plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old needs the root-power meaning made concrete before the number-classification rules, so the lesson moves from a hook, to a rule card and worked anatomy, to guided practice, then to the rational/irrational contrast and its traps, ending with a memory anchor. Each struggle-prone idea (a^(1/2) is not a/2, irrational sums can be rational) gets its own interactive or trap block.
coverage: Rewrite a^(1/n) as the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) as the nth root of a raised to m (or the mth power of the nth root)
Evaluate rational exponents on numbers, including negative bases and fractional results, and connect them to radical notation
Explain why the exponent rules (product, quotient, power) still work for rational exponents
Define rational numbers as ratios of integers with terminating or repeating decimals; irrational numbers as non-repeating, non-terminating decimals
Classify numbers as rational or irrational, including roots like sqrt(4) vs sqrt(2) and familiar constants like pi
State and justify the rules: rational + rational = rational, rational + irrational = irrational, rational x irrational = irrational (nonzero rational), irration
Recognize the common error of assuming every sum or product involving an irrational is irrational, and the error of treating a^(1/2) as a/2
Use rational-exponent and rational/irrational reasoning to simplify and estimate expressions

blocks.purpose: Open with the surprising fact that a^(1/2) is a root, not half, grabbing attention and surfacing the misconception before it hardens.

data.caption: An exponent of 1/2 asks for a square root. It does not cut the number in half.
data.context: Half of 16 is 8, so 16^(1/2) looks like it should be 8. It is not. The fraction 1/2 in the exponent means root, and the square root of 16 is 4. The same idea runs through every rational exponent you will meet today.

blocks.purpose: Give the anchor definition: a^(1/n) = nth root of a and a^(m/n) = nth root of a^m, with the three prerequisite facts (root meaning, power meaning, exponent rules).

data.ruleName: Rational exponents are roots and powers
data.anchor: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, and a^(m/n) is the nth root of a raised to the m.
prerequisites: The nth root of a is the number that, raised to the nth power, gives a (for even n, the nonnegative one): the cube root of 8 is 2 because 2^3 = 8.
A positive whole-number exponent means repeated multiplication: a^m is a multiplied by itself m times.
For positive bases, the exponent rules still hold: a^p times a^q = a^(p+q), a^p divided by a^q = a^(p-q), and (a^p)^q = a^(pq).
A negative exponent means reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1 divided by a^(m/n), so 4^(-1/2) = 1/2.

blocks.purpose: Break down a worked example like 8^(2/3) and 16^(1/2) part by part so learners see which number is the root and which is the power.

data.title: Anatomy of 8^(2/3)
data.caption: The denominator of the exponent tells you which root to take. The numerator tells you the power.

labels.pickerAria: Choose a part of the expression 8^(2/3)
labels.emptyHint: Tap a part of the expression to see what it does.

parts.label: The base, 8
parts.description: The base is the number you take a root of and then raise to a power.

parts.label: The denominator, 3
parts.description: The bottom of the fraction is the root. A 3 means cube root.
parts.example: The cube root of 8 is 2, because 2 times 2 times 2 = 8.

parts.label: The numerator, 2
parts.description: The top of the fraction is the power you raise the root to.

parts.label: The fraction bar
parts.role: Joins root and power, root first
parts.description: The bar joins the root and the power in one exponent. Take the root first to keep the numbers small, then apply the power.
parts.example: 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4. Doing it the other way, 8^2 = 64, and the cube root of 64 is also 4.

blocks.purpose: Have learners type the radical or rational-exponent equivalent and evaluate simple cases, retrieving the root-power conversion rather than rereading it.

data.prompt: Write 27^(2/3) as a radical expression, then evaluate it. Type the final value.
data.context: Remember: the denominator of the exponent is the root, and the numerator is the power.
data.successMessage: Correct. The cube root of 27 is 3, and 3^2 = 9.
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Take the cube root of 27 first, then square the result.
data.explanation: 27^(2/3) = (cube root of 27)^2 = 3^2 = 9. Taking the root first keeps the numbers small.

blocks.purpose: Contrast rational numbers (ratio of integers, terminating or repeating decimals) with irrational numbers (non-repeating, non-terminating), including sqrt(4) vs sqrt(2) and pi.

data.title: Rational versus irrational numbers
data.subtitle: The decimal tells the story: rational decimals settle down, irrational decimals never do.

items.label: Ratio of integers
items.text: A rational number can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not zero.

items.label: Decimals that settle
items.text: The decimal either terminates or repeats a block forever.

items.label: Roots of perfect squares
items.text: The square root of a perfect square is a whole number, so it is rational.
items.example: sqrt(4) = 2, which is rational.

items.label: Approximations of pi
items.text: Decimals and fractions that approximate pi are rational, even though pi is not.
items.example: 3.14 = 314/100 and 22/7 are both rational.

items.label: Not a ratio of integers
items.text: No fraction of two integers equals an irrational number.
items.example: sqrt(2) cannot be written as a/b.

items.label: Decimals that never settle
items.text: The decimal never ends and never repeats a block.
items.example: sqrt(2) = 1.41421356... keeps going with no pattern.

items.label: Roots of non-perfect squares
items.text: The square root of a positive integer is irrational unless that integer is a perfect square.
items.example: sqrt(2) is irrational; sqrt(9) = 3 is rational.

items.label: Famous constants
items.text: pi is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
items.example: pi = 3.14159... never ends or repeats.

data.footnote: A decimal that looks random is not automatically irrational. Check whether it repeats: 0.121212... is rational because it equals 4/33.

blocks.purpose: Sort a mixed set of numbers and expressions into rational vs irrational buckets, applying the definitions to roots and constants.

data.title: Sort each number
data.instruction: Decide whether each number is rational or irrational, then place it in the correct bucket.

categories.label: Rational
categories.hint: Can be written as a ratio of integers; decimal terminates or repeats.

categories.label: Irrational
categories.hint: Cannot be written as a ratio of integers; decimal never ends or repeats.

items.text: sqrt(4)
sqrt(2)
pi
sqrt(10)

blocks.purpose: Lay out the sum and product rules side by side: rational+rational, rational+irrational, rational x irrational, and the either-case for irrational+irrational and irrational x irrational.

data.title: What happens when you add or multiply?
data.subtitle: Rational numbers are closed under addition and multiplication. Irrational numbers are not.

items.label: rational + rational
items.text: Adding two rational numbers gives a rational number.
items.example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, which is rational.

items.label: rational x rational
items.text: Multiplying two rational numbers gives a rational number.
items.example: (2/3) times (9/4) = 3/2, which is rational.

items.label: rational + irrational
items.text: Adding a rational to an irrational always gives an irrational.
items.example: 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational. If it equaled a rational s, then sqrt(2) = s - 1 would be rational, which is false.

items.label: nonzero rational x irrational
items.text: Multiplying an irrational by a nonzero rational always gives an irrational.
items.example: 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational. If it equaled s, then sqrt(2) = s/3 would be rational.

items.label: irrational + irrational
items.text: The sum can be rational or irrational, so you must check.
items.example: sqrt(2) + (-sqrt(2)) = 0 is rational, but sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) is irrational.

items.label: irrational x irrational
items.text: The product can be rational or irrational, so you must check.
items.example: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2 is rational, but sqrt(2) times sqrt(3) = sqrt(6) is irrational.

items.label: zero times irrational
items.text: Zero is the exception to the product rule.
items.example: 0 times pi = 0, which is rational.

items.label: The trap
items.text: Do not assume every expression with an irrational is irrational.
items.example: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2 shows the assumption fails.

data.footnote: Rational + irrational is always irrational, and nonzero rational x irrational is always irrational. Two irrationals together need a check.

blocks.purpose: Target the #1 mistake: assuming every sum or product with an irrational is irrational, and that a^(1/2) equals a/2, revealing why intuition fails.

data.question: Which of these expressions is rational?
data.context: Look at each expression carefully. One of them simplifies to a rational number.
data.commonErrorLabel: Assuming every expression with an irrational is irrational

trapReasons.0: Two irrationals can add to a rational, but sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) does not. It stays irrational.
trapReasons.2: A nonzero rational times an irrational is always irrational, so 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational.
trapReasons.3: A rational plus an irrational is always irrational, so 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: It feels like any expression containing an irrational must be irrational. But two irrationals can cancel or combine into a rational. Here sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2, because squaring undoes the square root.
data.correctReasoning: sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) = 2, and 2 is a ratio of integers (2/1), so it is rational. The other three choices stay irrational: sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) is irrational, 3 times sqrt(2) is irrational, and 1 + sqrt(2) is irrational.
data.recoveryTip: Before calling an expression irrational, try to simplify it. If the irrational parts multiply to a perfect square or cancel by addition, the result may be rational.

facts.fact: a^(1/n) means the nth root of a; for example 9^(1/2) = 3 and 8^(1/3) = 2.
a^(m/n) equals (the nth root of a) raised to the m, which also equals the nth root of (a^m).
Example: 8^(2/3) = (cube root of 8)^2 = 2^2 = 4. Taking the root first keeps numbers small.
A negative exponent means reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1 / a^(m/n). Example: 4^(-1/2) = 1/2.
With an even root, a negative base has no real result: (-4)^(1/2) is not a real number. With an odd root it works: (-8)^(1/3) = -2.
Fractional results are fine: 27^(-2/3) = 1/9; 16^(3/4) = 8.

For rational exponents, the product rule a^p · a^q = a^(p+q) still works; e.g. 4^(1/2)·4^(3/2)=4^2=16. The quotient rule a^p / a^q = a^(p−q) and power rule (a^p)^q = a^(pq) also hold (for bases where the roots are real, usually a>0).
Why the rules work: defining a^(1/n) so that (a^(1/n))^n = a^(1/n · n) = a^1 is what makes the power rule keep holding; for example (a^(1/2))^2 = a.
A rational number can be written as a/b with integers a and b, b not zero.
facts.source_quote: In mathematics, a rational number is a number that can be expressed as the quotient or fraction p/q of two integers, a numerator p and a non-zero denominator q.

facts.fact: Rational numbers have decimals that terminate or repeat (0.25, 0.333...).
Irrational numbers cannot be written as a ratio of integers; their decimals never end and never repeat.
sqrt(4)=2 is rational; sqrt(2) is irrational; pi is irrational. The square root of a positive integer is irrational unless it is a perfect square.
Rational + rational is rational, and rational × rational is rational (closure).
Rational + irrational is always irrational. Proof: if r + x = s were rational, x = s − r would be rational, a contradiction.
Nonzero rational × irrational is irrational. Proof: if r·x = s, then x = s/r would be rational. Zero times an irrational is 0, which is rational.
The sum or product of two irrational numbers can be rational or irrational: sqrt(2)·sqrt(2)=2 and sqrt(2)+(−sqrt(2))=0 are rational, while sqrt(2)+sqrt(3) and sqrt(2)·sqrt(3)=sqrt(6) are irrational.
Common error: a^(1/2) is the square root of a, not a/2. Example: 16^(1/2)=4, not 8.
Common error: believing every sum or product involving an irrational is irrational; 0·pi = 0 and sqrt(2)·sqrt(2)=2 are counterexamples.
Estimating: 10^(1/2) is between 3 and 4, near 3.16, because 9<10<16. 20^(1/2) is about 4.5.
Decimal approximations like 3.14 or 22/7 for pi are rational approximations; pi itself is irrational.

plans.approach: This lesson introduces algebraic structure vocabulary through a clear progression: hook curiosity by contrasting calculation vs structure, define core terms with a rule card and interactive jargon buster, show a worked parse, then give varied retrieval practice before a mnemonic anchor locks it in. The sequence respects prerequisite order (vocabulary before parsing) and spaces retrieval across blo
coverage: Expressions as structured objects (not just calculations)
Terms: parts separated by + or –
Factors: quantities multiplied within a term
Coefficients: numerical factor of a term with a variable
Distinguishing terms from factors
Distinguishing coefficients from constants
Precise vocabulary: term, factor, coefficient, constant, variable
Reading an expression by naming its structural parts

blocks.purpose: Present two conflicting readings of 3x² + 5x – 7 (calculate vs describe structure) to spark curiosity about algebraic language.

data.prompt: Two students look at 3x^2 + 5x - 7. Which reading gets you further?
data.context: One student treats the expression as a job to finish. The other treats it as an object with parts to name. Both readings are useful, but seeing structure helps with combining, factoring and solving.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: Run the calculation
leftChoice.body: Plug in a number for x, do the arithmetic, and report a single answer. The expression is a set of instructions to carry out.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Describe the structure
rightChoice.body: Name the parts: three terms, each with its own factors. The variable terms also have coefficients. The expression is an object you can take apart and talk about.

data.footerNote: Keep both readings in mind. This lesson trains the second one.

blocks.purpose: Define term, factor, coefficient, constant, variable with a bold anchor sentence and three prerequisite bullets for each.

data.ruleName: The Five Words That Describe Any Expression
data.anchor: An expression is an object built from terms, and each term is built from factors, with a coefficient leading any variable part.
prerequisites: A term is a number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables, and terms are separated by addition or subtraction signs.
A factor is a quantity multiplied with others inside a term, so terms are added while factors are multiplied.
A coefficient is the numerical factor of a term that contains a variable, and a constant is a term with no variable whose value never changes.

terms.label: term
terms.definition: A number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables; terms are separated by plus or minus signs.
terms.hint: In 5x(y + 1) + 4 there are two terms: 5x(y + 1) and 4.

terms.label: factors
terms.definition: Quantities that are multiplied together inside a term.
terms.hint: Terms are added; factors are multiplied.

terms.label: coefficient
terms.definition: The numerical factor of a term that contains a variable.
terms.hint: In -x the coefficient is -1, and in x it is 1.

data.footer: Notice that 5x(y + 1) is one term, not two, because its parts are multiplied. The addition is inside the parentheses, which count as one factor.

blocks.purpose: Split card comparing a flawed 'calculate first' reading to a correct structural description of the same expression.

data.conceptSubtitle: Same expression, two very different readings
data.prompt: Sweep the divider to compare the two readings of 4x - 7.

before.label: Before
before.title: Calculate first
before.body: Substitute a value for x, multiply, subtract 7, and stop there. The expression is only a set of instructions to carry out.
points: The minus sign is treated as an operation between 4x and 7
Nothing is learned about how the expression is built

after.label: After
after.title: Describe the structure
after.body: Read subtraction as adding the opposite. The expression has two terms, 4x and -7. The term 4x has factors 4 and x, with coefficient 4. The constant term is -7.
points: The sign belongs to the term, so the constant is -7

data.footerNote: Naming the parts is what lets you combine, factor, and solve later.

blocks.purpose: Numbered worked example parsing 4y³ – 2y + 9 into terms, then factors and coefficients of each term.

data.title: Worked example: parse 4y^3 - 2y + 9
data.subtitle: Name the terms first, then open each term up.

steps.label: Step 1: Find the terms
steps.text: Split at the plus and minus signs, and keep each sign with the term that follows it.
steps.detail: The terms are 4y^3, -2y, and 9. There are three terms.

steps.label: Step 2: Open the first term
steps.text: The term 4y^3 has factors 4, y, y, and y, so its coefficient is 4.
steps.detail: The variable part is y^3, and the numerical factor in front of it is 4.

steps.label: Step 3: Open the second term
steps.text: The term -2y has factors -2 and y, so its coefficient is -2.
steps.detail: The negative sign travels with the term, so the coefficient is negative.

steps.label: Step 4: Name the last term
steps.text: The term 9 has no variable, so it is the constant term.
steps.detail: A constant is a term, but it is not a coefficient, because no variable is attached to it.

steps.label: Step 5: Say it in one sentence
steps.text: 4y^3 - 2y + 9 has three terms: 4y^3 with coefficient 4, -2y with coefficient -2, and the constant 9.
steps.detail: This sentence is a full structural description of the expression.

facts.fact: A term is a number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables; terms in an expression are separated by addition or subtraction signs.
A factor is a quantity multiplied with others inside a term.
A coefficient is the numerical factor of a term that contains a variable.
A constant is a term with no variable; its value never changes.
A variable is a letter that stands for a number that can change or is unknown.
In 3x + 5, there are two terms: 3x and 5. 3x has factors 3 and x; coefficient 3; 5 is the constant.
Subtraction can be read as adding the opposite, so in 4x - 7 the terms are 4x and -7, and the constant term is -7.
In -x + 2y, the coefficient of x is -1, and in x the coefficient is 1 (it is usually not written).
Terms are added or subtracted; factors are multiplied. In 2(x+3), the whole thing is one term with factors 2 and (x+3).
In 5x(y+1) + 4, there are two terms; the first has factors 5, x, and (y+1).
Like terms have the same variable parts, such as 3x and 7x; constants are also like terms with each other.
A coefficient is a factor, but not every factor is a coefficient; in 3xy the coefficient of xy is 3, while x and y are variable factors.
A constant like 5 is a term, but it is not called a coefficient because it has no variable attached.
Some textbooks say coefficient can mean any factor relative to the rest (e.g., 3 is the coefficient of xy, x is the coefficient of 3y); in Algebra 1 the numerical meaning is standard.
Common Core standard A-SSE.A.1 asks students to interpret expressions by viewing parts such as terms, factors, and coefficients.

misconceptions: Thinking an expression is only a calculation to carry out rather than an object with parts.
Thinking the terms of 4x - 7 are 4x and 7 (the sign belongs to the term: -7).
Confusing terms and factors: in 3x + 5 the 3 is not a term; 3x is.
Thinking 2(x+3) has two terms; it is one term with two factors.
Calling the constant 5 in 3x + 5 a coefficient.
Believing x has no coefficient; it is 1.
Ignoring the negative sign when naming the coefficient of -x or -4y.
Thinking a variable must be x; any letter can be a variable.

plans.approach: A typical learner needs the concrete picture first, so the lesson builds from single half-planes to the overlap, then to corner points and the best vertex, with retrieval and a misconception trap before the summary. Each block does a distinct job: hook, rule, worked flow, practice, trap, anchor.
coverage: Graph a linear inequality in two variables: solid vs dashed boundary line and which side to shade
A system of inequalities is the overlap of two or more half-planes; the solution is the intersection
Feasible region: the shaded overlap that satisfies every constraint at once
Test-point method to decide which side of a boundary to shade
Vertices (corner points) of a feasible region and how to find them by solving pairs of boundary equations
Evaluate an objective value at each vertex and pick the best (max or min)
Translate a real-world constraint problem into inequalities plus non-negativity conditions
Common errors: shading the union instead of the overlap, wrong solid/dashed, forgetting x≥0, y≥0, testing a point on the line

blocks.purpose: Pose a real scheduling problem (hours on two jobs under pay and time limits) where two constraints conflict, so the learner feels why an overlap region answers 'what's possible'.

data.prompt: You can work two part-time jobs this week, but you only have 20 hours free. Which plan do you pick?
data.context: Job A pays $10 an hour and Job B pays $15 an hour. Your goal is to earn at least $200, and you cannot work more than 20 hours total. Both plans look tempting. Check each one against the limits.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: Work 20 hours at Job B
leftChoice.body: 20 hours at $15 earns $300, which clears the $200 goal and uses exactly 20 hours. But all your time goes to one job.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Split 10 hours each
rightChoice.body: 10 hours at each job earns $100 + $150 = $250 and uses exactly 20 hours. This one fits both limits too.

data.footerNote: Some plans fail a limit. The plans that satisfy every limit at once form a shaded region on a graph, and that region is what this lesson is about.

blocks.purpose: State the anchor rule: a system's solution is the overlap of half-planes, with solid vs dashed boundary and the test-point check as prerequisites.

data.anchor: The solution of a system of inequalities is the overlap of the half-planes: a point is a solution only if it makes every inequality in the system true at the same time.
prerequisites: A single linear inequality graphs as a half-plane, bounded by the line from its related equation.
Use a solid boundary for ≤ or ≥, because points on the line are solutions; use a dashed boundary for < or >, because they are not.
To choose a side, test a point that is not on the line, such as (0,0), and shade the side where the inequality comes out true.

blocks.purpose: Walk the procedure: graph each boundary, decide solid/dashed, test a point, shade, then find where boundaries cross.

data.title: Graphing a System, Step by Step
data.subtitle: Follow the same path for each inequality, then look for where the shaded parts agree.

nodes.label: Start with the system

blocks.purpose: Learner sorts boundary lines and shaded sides into correct/incorrect for given inequalities, practising solid vs dashed and side choice.

data.title: Sort the Graphing Moves
data.instruction: Each card describes a move for graphing one inequality. Sort it into the bucket where it belongs.

categories.label: Correct move
categories.hint: This is what the rule says to do.

items.text: For y < 2x + 1, draw a dashed boundary line.
items.detail: The sign is <, so the line itself is excluded.

items.text: For y ≥ -x + 4, draw a solid boundary line.
items.detail: The sign is ≥, so the line itself is included.

items.text: For 3x + 2y ≤ 12, test (0,0) and shade the side where it is true.
items.detail: (0,0) is not on the line, so it gives real information.

items.text: For y > x - 5, draw a solid boundary line.
items.detail: A solid line would wrongly include the boundary points.

items.text: For 2x + y < 6, test the point (3,0) to pick a side.
items.detail: (3,0) lies on the line 2x + y = 6, so the test tells you nothing.

items.text: For y ≤ -2x + 3, shade above the line because the sign points up.
items.detail: With y isolated, ≤ means shade below the line.

blocks.purpose: Label a graphed system: each boundary, the feasible region, and its vertices, so the learner sees the overlap and corner points explicitly.

data.title: Anatomy of a Feasible Region
data.caption: The system is y ≥ 0, x ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 6, and y ≤ 2x. The shaded overlap is the feasible region, and its corners are the vertices.

parts.label: Boundary line x + y = 6
parts.description: This line comes from the inequality x + y ≤ 6. It passes through (0,6) and (6,0). Because the sign is ≤, the line is solid, and the shaded side is the one containing (0,0), which gives 0 ≤ 6, a true statement.
parts.example: Test (0,0): 0 + 0 = 0, and 0 ≤ 6 is true, so shade the side with the origin.

parts.label: Boundary line y = 2x
parts.description: This line comes from y ≤ 2x. The sign is ≤, so the line is solid. The origin is on this line, so it is a bad test point. Use (0,1) instead: 1 ≤ 0 is false, so the region lies below the line.
parts.example: Test (0,1): 1 ≤ 2(0) is false, so shade the other side, below y = 2x.

parts.label: Feasible region
parts.description: The feasible region is every point that satisfies all four constraints at once. It is the overlap of the four half-planes, not the union of them.
parts.example: The point (1,1) works: 1 ≥ 0, 1 ≥ 0, 1 + 1 = 2 ≤ 6, and 1 ≤ 2(1). The point (5,5) fails because 5 + 5 = 10 is not ≤ 6.

parts.label: Vertex (0, 0)
parts.description: Where x = 0 meets y = 0. Solving that pair gives (0,0), and it satisfies all four constraints, so it is a true vertex.
parts.example: x = 0 and y = 0 give (0,0). Check: 0 + 0 ≤ 6 and 0 ≤ 0, both true.

parts.label: Vertex (2, 4)
parts.description: Where y = 2x meets x + y = 6. Substitute: x + 2x = 6, so 3x = 6 and x = 2, then y = 4.
parts.example: Solve y = 2x with x + y = 6: x + 2x = 6, x = 2, y = 4. Check 2 + 4 ≤ 6, true.

parts.label: Vertex (6, 0)
parts.description: Where x + y = 6 meets y = 0. Setting y = 0 gives x = 6. This point also satisfies y ≤ 2x, since 0 ≤ 12, so it is a true vertex.
parts.example: At (6,0): 6 + 0 = 6 ≤ 6 and 0 ≤ 2(6) = 12, so it satisfies every constraint.

data.question: A student graphs the system y ≥ x and y ≤ -x + 4. They shade everything above y = x and everything below y = -x + 4, then call the whole shaded picture the solution. What is wrong?
data.context: The two boundary lines cross at (2, 2). The student's shading covers a large area, but the solution set is only the part shaded by both inequalities.
choices: Nothing is wrong; every shaded point is a solution.
The solution is only the overlap: the wedge to the left of (2,2) that is shaded by both inequalities.
The solution is the two boundary lines themselves.
The solution is the region shaded by neither inequality.
data.commonErrorLabel: Shading the union instead of the overlap

trapReasons.0: Shading looks like one big picture, so it is tempting to accept all of it. But a point in only one half-plane fails the other inequality.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Shading each inequality separately makes a large, connected picture, and it feels like the answer. But a system asks for points that satisfy every inequality at once, so only the part shaded twice counts.
data.correctReasoning: Test (0,3): y ≥ x gives 3 ≥ 0, true, and y ≤ -x + 4 gives 3 ≤ 4, true, so (0,3) is in. Test (3,0): y ≥ x gives 0 ≥ 3, false, so (3,0) is out even though it sits in the other half-plane. The points that pass both form a wedge with its corner at (2,2), opening to the left.
data.recoveryTip: After shading, pick one point from the wide shaded area and test it in every inequality. If it fails even one, it is not in the solution.

blocks.purpose: Micro-case: a small business with two constraints; evaluate the objective at each vertex and pick the best value, connecting vertices to the real decision.

data.ruleName: Best Vertex of a Feasible Region
data.headline: A small print shop finds its best profit at a corner, not the middle
data.caseText:
A print shop makes posters and flyers. Each poster earns $4 profit and each flyer earns $2. The shop has 12 hours of press time: a poster takes 2 hours and a flyer takes 1 hour, so 2x + y ≤ 12. Paper limits total output to x + y ≤ 8. Both x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 apply.

The feasible region has four corners: (0,0), (0,8), (4,4), and (6,0). The profit is P = 4x + 2y.

At (0,0), P = 0. At (0,8), P = 16. At (4,4), P = 16 + 8 = 24. At (6,0), P = 24. The best value is $24, reached at both (4,4) and (6,0).

The owner who guesses the middle of the region might pick (3,3) for P = 12 + 6 = 18, which is worse than the best corners, $24. Checking every vertex is what finds the true maximum.

metric.label: maximum profit, found at a vertex of the feasible region

data.consequenceMissed: Guessing a point in the middle of the region can miss the best profit by several dollars a week.
data.consequenceApplied: Evaluating P = 4x + 2y at every vertex proves $24 is the highest possible profit.
data.sourceNote: Profit and time figures are a made-up example built to show the vertex method.

facts.fact: The graph of a linear inequality in two variables is a half-plane bounded by the line from the related equation.
Use a solid boundary line for ≤ or ≥, because points on the line are solutions.
Use a dashed boundary line for < or >, because points on the line are not solutions.
To test a side, pick a point not on the line (like (0,0) if the line misses it), substitute it, and shade that side if the inequality is true, otherwise shade the other side.
A point on the boundary line is a bad test point because it gives no information about which side to shade.
For y > mx + b shade above the line, and for y < mx + b shade below; this shortcut works only when y is isolated with a positive coefficient.
A system of inequalities is two or more inequalities considered together; its solution set is the points that satisfy all of them, the intersection (overlap) of the half-planes.
In a constraint problem, the feasible region is the set of all points satisfying every constraint at once.

Vertices of the feasible region are corner points where boundary lines meet; find each by solving the pair of boundary equations (substitution or elimination) and check it satisfies the other constraints.
The objective function is the quantity to maximize or minimize, such as profit P = ax + by.
For a bounded feasible region, a linear objective function reaches its max and min at vertices, so evaluate it at each vertex and compare.
Real-world quantities like items or hours cannot be negative, so add x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, which limit the region to the first quadrant.
To translate a problem, define variables, write each limit (time, money, space) as an inequality, add non-negativity, then graph.
Whether answers must be whole numbers (e.g., cannot make 2.5 chairs) is a context decision; a vertex with fractional coordinates may not be allowed.

misconceptions: Shading the union (everything shaded by any inequality) instead of only the overlap.
Using a solid line for < or > (or dashed for ≤ or ≥).
Forgetting x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 in real-world problems.
Using a test point that lies on the boundary line.
Always shading above the line regardless of the inequality sign, especially after dividing by a negative or when y is not isolated.
Thinking the best value is at the middle of the region rather than a vertex.
Taking an intersection of two lines as a vertex without checking it satisfies all other constraints.
Thinking the vertex coordinates, not the objective value, are the answer to 'maximum profit'.

plans.approach: The sequence moves from the learner's existing procedural fluency to explicit justification, using a dilemma hook to create a need for reasoning, then modeling, error analysis, and progressive practice to build the habit of naming properties at each step. Checks target the most common gaps—identifying properties, supplying justifications, and constructing full argued solutions—immediately after th
coverage: Recognize that solving an equation is a logical argument where each step must be justified
Identify and name the Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division Properties of Equality
Apply the Distributive Property and combining like terms as justified steps
Write a step-by-step solution to a linear equation, citing the property for each step

blocks.purpose: Present two conflicting approaches—'just solve it' vs 'justify every step'—to spark curiosity about why algebraic justification matters and connect to prior equation-solving experience.

data.prompt: Two students solve 3(x + 2) = 21. Both get x = 5. One shows only the answer. The other shows every step with a reason. Which work would you rather hand in?
data.context: Your teacher says answers alone earn half credit this year. The other half comes from naming the reason for each step.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: Just solve it
leftChoice.body: Write 3(x + 2) = 21, then 3x + 6 = 21, then 3x = 15, then x = 5. No reasons given. Fast, and the answer is right.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Justify every step
rightChoice.body: Write the same four lines. Next to the first write "given", and next to each other line name the property that allows it: Distributive Property, Subtraction Property of Equality, Division Property of Equality.

data.footerNote: Keep both in mind. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write the right-hand version yourself, and you will see why it is worth the extra lines.

blocks.purpose: Define the four Properties of Equality with a bold anchor sentence and three prerequisite bullets, giving learners a clean reference for the core justifications they will use.

data.anchor: If two expressions are equal, then adding, subtracting, multiplying by, or dividing by the same nonzero number on both sides keeps them equal.
prerequisites: An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal, and a solution is a value of the variable that makes the statement true.
The Distributive Property, a(b + c) = ab + ac, rewrites one side of an equation; it is a property of arithmetic, not a property of equality.
Combining like terms such as 3x + 2x = 5x is also a rewrite of one side, justified by the Distributive Property.

blocks.purpose: Model a complete worked example of solving a linear equation, showing each step numbered and paired with its justifying property.

data.title: One equation, every step justified
data.subtitle: Solve 2(x + 3) = 14 and name the reason for each line.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.detail: This is the given equation. It is the starting point, so its reason is simply 'given'.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.detail: Distributive Property: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6. This rewrites the left side only, so it is a property of arithmetic.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.detail: Subtraction Property of Equality: subtract 6 from both sides, since 14 - 6 = 8. Both sides stay equal.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.detail: Division Property of Equality: divide both sides by 2, since 8 divided by 2 is 4. Dividing by 2 is allowed because 2 is not zero.

steps.label: Step 5
steps.detail: Substitution Property of Equality: replace x with 4 in the original equation. Both sides equal 14, so x = 4 is correct.

facts.fact: An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal; a solution is a value of the variable that makes it true.
Solving an equation is a chain of logical steps, and each step needs a reason such as a property, definition, or given fact.
Addition Property of Equality: if a = b, then a + c = b + c.
Subtraction Property of Equality: if a = b, then a - c = b - c.
Multiplication Property of Equality: if a = b, then ac = bc.
Division Property of Equality: if a = b and c ≠ 0, then a/c = b/c.
Doing the same operation to both sides keeps equality because both sides name the same number, so applying the same operation to that number gives the same result (like a balanced scale).
Multiplying or dividing both sides by 0 is not allowed as a reversible step: division by 0 is undefined, and multiplying by 0 turns any equation into 0 = 0, losing information.
Distributive Property: a(b + c) = ab + ac, and it also applies to subtraction: a(b - c) = ab - ac.
Combining like terms uses the Distributive Property (e.g., 3x + 2x = (3+2)x = 5x); like terms have the same variable part.
The Distributive, Commutative, Associative, Identity and Inverse Properties are properties of real-number arithmetic used to rewrite one side of an equation; properties of equality act on both sides.
Common error: incomplete distribution, e.g., 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4 is wrong; correct is 3x + 12.
Common error: a sign mistake, e.g., -(x - 5) becomes -x - 5 instead of -x + 5; or subtracting 7 from both sides of x + 7 = 2 and getting x = 9.

Dividing both sides by a variable expression (e.g., x) can lose solutions, since the expression might equal 0; for x² = 3x dividing by x loses x = 0. In linear equations at this level, divide only by nonzero numbers.
To verify a solution, substitute it into the original equation (not a later step) and check both sides simplify to the same number.
Checking in the original equation catches errors made in any step; checking a later line could hide an earlier mistake.
Example: 2(x + 3) = 14. Distributive: 2x + 6 = 14. Subtraction Property of Equality: 2x = 8. Division Property of Equality: x = 4. Check: 2(4+3)=14.
Substitution Property of Equality: if a = b, b can replace a in any expression or equation; it is the justification for checking a solution.
Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive Properties of Equality are other properties of equality, alongside the four operation properties.

misconceptions: Thinking you 'move' a term across the equals sign and change its sign, rather than adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides.
Thinking the Distributive Property is a property of equality; it is an arithmetic property used to rewrite one side.
Applying an operation to only one side.
Distributing a factor to only the first term in parentheses.
Dividing both sides by a variable expression without considering that it could be zero.
Checking the solution in a later step rather than the original equation.
Believing 'justify' means just describing the operation; the reason should name the property.

plans.approach: A typical learner needs a concrete hook, one clean rule card tying percent, mixture, and unit problems to the same equation idea, then guided practice and a trap that targets the two classic mistakes. The level ends with a compact cheat sheet and a memory anchor so the shared equation structure sticks.
coverage: Percent change as an equation: part = percent × whole, and percent change = (new − old)/old
Solving percent equations by isolating the unknown (finding the part, the whole, or the percent)
Mixture problems: amount × concentration = pure substance, and combining two mixtures into one equation
Unit conversion as a proportion or rate equation (e.g., 1 inch = 2.54 cm) with unit cancellation
Setting up an equation from a word problem: define the variable, translate the relationship, then solve
Checking answers for reasonableness (percent over 100%, units matching, mixture totals)
Common error: adding percents or concentrations directly instead of weighting by amounts
Common error: flipping the percent-change base (dividing by new instead of old) or mismatching units

blocks.purpose: Grab attention with a surprising real percent-change fact (e.g., a price that rises 50% then falls 50% does not return to start) to motivate why the equation matters.

data.caption: A store raises a $100 jacket by 50%, then later marks the new price down by 50%. The final price is $75, which is 75% of where it started.
data.context: Two changes of 50% in opposite directions do not cancel. The first 50% is taken of $100, but the second 50% is taken of $150, so the two percents have different bases.

blocks.purpose: State the anchor idea: every percent, mixture, and unit problem is one equation of the form part = rate × whole, with the three prerequisite pieces named.

data.anchor: Many percent, mixture, and unit problems rest on one idea: part = rate × whole.
prerequisites: You can solve a one-variable equation by undoing operations in reverse order.
You can write a percent as a decimal: 25% = 0.25, 7% = 0.07, 130% = 1.30.
You can multiply and divide fractions and decimals, and you know that multiplying by a fraction equal to 1 does not change a value.

blocks.purpose: Bridge the abstract part = rate × whole rule to everyday objects (a juice mix, a sale tag, a recipe conversion) so the structure feels concrete.

data.rule: In these problems, a rate acts on a whole to produce a part.
data.ruleDetail: Percent problems use a percent rate, mixture problems use a concentration, and unit problems use a conversion factor. The equation keeps the same basic shape.

analogies.everydayScene: You pour 2 liters of 10% juice concentrate and 3 liters of 20% concentrate into one pitcher.
analogies.because: Each bottle contributes its own liters times its own strength, and the pure juice amounts add while the liters add. The final strength is the total pure juice divided by the total liters.

analogies.everydayScene: A $40 backpack has a tag reading 25% off.
analogies.because: The discount is a part of the original $40 whole, and the rate is 0.25. The part is 0.25 × 40 = $10 off.

analogies.everydayScene: A recipe written in cups needs to be followed with a measuring cup marked in milliliters.
analogies.because: 1 US cup ≈ 236.6 mL, so the ratio (236.6 mL / 1 cup) equals 1 and changes the units without changing the amount.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the three equation templates side by side — percent change, mixture (amount × concentration), and unit conversion — with color-coded variable definitions.

data.title: Three templates, one structure
data.subtitle: Pick the template that matches the story, then fill in what you know.

variables.name: The piece you get
variables.definition: The amount produced by the rate: the discount, the pure substance, or the converted measurement.
variables.unit: same kind of unit as the whole, or the new unit after conversion

variables.name: The multiplier
variables.definition: A percent written as a decimal, a concentration written as a decimal, or a conversion factor such as 2.54 cm per inch.
variables.unit: decimal, or a ratio of two units
variables.note: Never drop a percent in as 25. Write 0.25.

variables.name: The base amount
variables.definition: What the rate acts on: the original price, the total liters of solution, or the starting measurement.
variables.unit: the unit you are starting from

data.footnote: Percent change is the same idea rearranged: percent change = (new − old) / old, and the old value is always the base.

blocks.purpose: Give a short numbered procedure for setting up any of these word problems: define the variable, write the relationship, substitute, solve, check units and reasonableness.

data.title: Set up any of these problems in five moves
data.subtitle: Works for percent, mixture, and unit questions alike.

steps.label: Name the variable
steps.text: Write what you are looking for, with its unit.
steps.detail: For example: let x = the original price in dollars, or let x = the number of liters of 20% solution.

steps.label: Write the relationship
steps.text: Translate the sentence into part = rate × whole, or into the matching template.
steps.detail: A percent increase of p% means new = old × (1 + p/100). A decrease means new = old × (1 − p/100).

steps.label: Match the units first
steps.text: Convert anything measured in different units before it enters the equation.
steps.detail: Minutes and hours, or inches and centimeters, cannot sit in the same equation until one is converted.

steps.label: Solve for the unknown
steps.text: Undo the operations in reverse order to isolate the variable.

steps.label: Check in context
steps.text: Ask whether the size and the units make sense.
steps.detail: A mixture's final concentration must land between the two starting concentrations, and a part of a whole cannot be more than 100% of that whole.

blocks.purpose: Let the learner practise writing and solving a percent-change equation by typing the missing values into a worked setup.

data.prompt: A bicycle costs $250 after a 20% discount. Fill in the equation that finds the original price, then give that price.
data.context: Let x = the original price in dollars. The sale price is the original price times (1 − 0.20). So 0.80x = 250.
data.placeholder: Type the original price in dollars
data.successMessage: Correct. Dividing 250 by 0.80 gives 312.50, and 20% off 312.50 is indeed 250.
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Divide 250 by 0.80, not by 0.20, because the sale price is 80% of the original.

blocks.purpose: Confront the top misconception: adding two concentrations directly instead of weighting by amounts, and reveal why intuition fails.

data.question: What is the concentration of the combined mixture?
data.context: You mix 2 liters of a 10% salt solution with 3 liters of a 20% salt solution.
data.commonErrorLabel: Adding concentrations directly instead of weighting by amount

trapReasons.1: Adding 10% and 20% gives 30%, which is higher than either solution, so it can't be right. Concentrations are not amounts, so they can't be added.

facts.fact: Part = percent × whole, with the percent written as a decimal or fraction (25% = 0.25).
To find the percent, divide part by whole; to find the whole, divide part by the decimal percent.
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old, then multiplied by 100 to give a percent.
A positive percent change is an increase; a negative one is a decrease. The base is always the old (original) value.
A percent increase of p% gives new = old × (1 + p/100); a decrease gives new = old × (1 − p/100).
A percent can exceed 100% (for example, a quantity that triples has increased 200%), but a part of a whole cannot exceed 100% of that whole.
A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the start, because the two percents have different bases (result is 96% of the original).
Mixture: amount of solution × concentration (as decimal) = amount of pure substance.
Combining mixtures: pure substance adds and total amounts add, but concentrations do not add or simply average. Equation: a1·c1 + a2·c2 = (a1 + a2)·c_final.
Example: 2 L of 10% plus 3 L of 20% gives 0.2 + 0.6 = 0.8 L pure in 5 L, which is 16% (not 30% or 15%).
The final concentration of a mixture lies between the two starting concentrations, a useful reasonableness check.
1 inch = 2.54 centimeters exactly, by international agreement.
Unit conversion multiplies by a conversion factor equal to 1, such as (2.54 cm / 1 in), arranged so unwanted units cancel.
Example: 10 in × 2.54 cm/in = 25.4 cm; the inch units cancel.
Setting up word problems: define the variable with units, translate the relationship into an equation, solve, then check in the original context.
Mismatched units (e.g., minutes vs. hours) must be converted before using them in one equation.

misconceptions: Adding percents or concentrations directly (10% + 20% = 30%) instead of weighting by amounts.
Dividing the change by the new value instead of the old value.
Thinking a 20% rise then a 20% drop returns to the original.
Thinking percent can never exceed 100%.
Using the percent as 25 instead of 0.25 in equations.
Flipping the conversion factor so units don't cancel.
Averaging two concentrations without regard to the amounts.

plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old needs the AND/OR distinction made concrete before notation, so the lesson opens with a real choice, builds the intersection/union idea with a Venn-style contrast, then practices solving and graphing before consolidating with a cheat sheet. Retrieval and trap blocks target the two classic errors: mixing up AND/OR and forgetting the sign flip.
coverage: Compound inequality = two inequalities joined by AND or OR
AND means intersection: solutions must satisfy both parts simultaneously
OR means union: solutions satisfy at least one part
Solve each part separately using inverse operations, then combine
Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign in each part
Graph AND solutions as the overlap of two rays (a bounded segment)
Graph OR solutions as both rays extending outward (unbounded, two directions)
Write AND solutions as a < x < b and in interval notation (a, b)
Write OR solutions with two separate inequalities and union notation using ∪
Recognize no-solution AND (empty set) and all-real OR cases
Common error: treating AND like OR, or forgetting to flip signs on negatives

blocks.purpose: Pose a real ride-height or temperature scenario where a value must satisfy two conditions at once versus either of two conditions, sparking the AND vs OR question.

data.prompt: A theme-park ride has a safety rule: you may ride only if your height is at least 48 inches and at most 78 inches. A second ride says you may ride if you are under 40 inches or over 60 inches. Which rule is the harder one to satisfy?
data.context: Both rules use two numbers, but the little word between them changes everything. One rule asks you to clear two bars at once. The other asks you to clear just one of two bars.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: At least 48 and at most 78
leftChoice.body: You must be tall enough AND not too tall. Both conditions have to hold at the same time, so only the heights in the middle work.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Under 40 or over 60
rightChoice.body: You need only one condition to hold. A height of 30 inches works, and so does a height of 70 inches, but 50 inches works for neither.

data.footerNote: Keep both rules in mind. The word and squeezes the answers together; the word or pulls them apart.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side contrast of AND (intersection, must meet both) versus OR (union, meets at least one), with plain-language anchors.

data.title: AND versus OR: two words, two different solution sets
data.subtitle: A compound inequality is two inequalities joined by and or by or. The joining word decides which numbers count.

items.label: Both parts at once
items.text: A number is a solution only if it makes both inequalities true at the same time.
items.example: x > 2 and x < 5: the number 4 works, but 6 fails the second part.

items.label: Picture the overlap
items.text: Graph each part as a ray, then keep only where the two rays overlap. When the rays point toward each other, the overlap is a segment between two endpoints.
items.example: x > 2 and x < 5 shades only the stretch between 2 and 5.

items.label: Shorthand chain
items.text: When the smaller number sits on the left, you may write the two parts as one chain.
items.example: 2 < x < 5 means x > 2 and x < 5.

items.label: Interval notation
items.text: Write the two endpoints in order inside parentheses, or use brackets for endpoints that are included.

items.label: At least one part
items.text: A number is a solution if it makes either inequality true. It counts even if it makes both true.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3: -5 works, 3 works, and 0 works for neither.

items.label: Picture two rays
items.text: Graph each part as a ray and keep everything either ray covers. The arrows point in opposite directions and the middle stays unshaded.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3 shades left of -1 and right of 3, with a gap between.

items.label: No chain allowed
items.text: An or solution cannot be squeezed into one chain like a < x < b, because the middle numbers are not solutions.
items.example: Writing 3 <= x < -1 for x < -1 or x >= 3 is wrong.

items.label: Interval notation with union
items.text: Write each piece in interval notation and join them with the union symbol, which looks like a U.
items.example: x < -1 or x >= 3 is (-infinity, -1) U [3, infinity).

data.footnote: Ask yourself one question: must a number pass both tests, or is passing one test enough? Both means and; one is enough means or.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the procedure: solve each part with inverse operations, flip sign on negative multiply/divide, then combine by overlap (AND) or joining (OR).

data.title: How to solve any compound inequality
data.subtitle: Work on each part with inverse operations, then combine the results with the joining word.

steps.label: Split the parts
steps.text: Separate the compound inequality into its two simple inequalities, or keep a three-part inequality lined up as three parts.
steps.detail: x + 3 < 7 and 2x >= 10 becomes two separate problems to solve.

steps.label: Undo addition and subtraction
steps.text: Add or subtract the same number on both sides of each part. Adding or subtracting a negative does not change the direction of the sign.
steps.detail: x - (-4) < 1 becomes x + 4 < 1, then x < -3. The sign stays <.

steps.label: Undo multiplication and division
steps.text: Multiply or divide each part by the same number. If that number is negative, reverse the inequality sign in every part you touched.
steps.detail: -2x > 8 becomes x < -4, because dividing by -2 flips > to <.

steps.label: Combine with the joining word
steps.text: Keep and or or exactly as it was given. For and, the answer is the overlap; for or, the answer is everything either part covers.
steps.detail: x > 2 and x < 5 becomes 2 < x < 5. x < -1 or x >= 3 stays as two pieces.

steps.label: Check the edge cases

data.prompt: The inequality 4x + 1 < -3 or 2x - 5 >= 1 has been solved to x < -1 or x >= 3. Type its solution in interval notation.
data.context: x < -1 or x >= 3
data.successMessage: Correct. The open endpoint -1 takes a parenthesis, the included endpoint 3 takes a bracket, and the union symbol joins the two pieces.
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Check each endpoint: is -1 included or excluded, and is 3 included or excluded? Then join the two pieces with the union symbol.
data.explanation: x < -1 is (-infinity, -1) because -1 is not included and infinity always takes a parenthesis. x >= 3 is [3, infinity) because 3 is included. The word or means union, so join them with U: (-infinity, -1) U [3, infinity).

blocks.purpose: Target the #1 mistake: forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative inside a compound inequality.

data.question: Solve the compound inequality -2 < -3x + 4 <= 10. Which choice is correct?
data.commonErrorLabel: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative

trapReasons.0: The signs were left unflipped after dividing by -3, so the open and closed ends land on the wrong numbers.
trapReasons.2: The inequality is right, but 2 is not included, so the bracket at 2 should be a parenthesis.
trapReasons.3: The numbers were put in the wrong order while flipping signs, which makes an impossible chain.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Dividing by -3 feels like ordinary division, so it is easy to keep the signs pointing the same way. But dividing by a negative number reverses the order on the number line, so every inequality sign in the chain must turn around.
data.correctReasoning: Subtract 4 from all three parts: -6 < -3x <= 6. Divide all three parts by -3 and flip both signs: 2 > x >= -2. Rewrite with the smaller number on the left: -2 <= x < 2, which is [-2, 2). Check: x = -2 gives 10, which works. x = 2 gives -2, which fails -2 < -2.
data.recoveryTip: Before you divide, circle the sign of the number you are dividing by. If it is negative, flip every inequality sign, then reorder the chain so the smallest number sits on the left. Test both endpoints at the end.

facts.fact: A compound inequality is two inequalities joined by the word and or the word or.
An AND compound inequality is true only for values that satisfy both parts at the same time; its solution set is the intersection of the two solution sets.
An OR compound inequality is true for values that satisfy at least one part; its solution set is the union of the two solution sets.
To solve a compound inequality, solve each part separately with inverse operations, then combine the results with and or or.
Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign; do this in each part that needs it.
Adding or subtracting a negative number does not reverse the inequality sign.
The graph of an AND solution is the overlap of two rays, which is a bounded segment between two endpoints (or a single ray if one ray lies inside the other).
The graph of an OR solution with arrows pointing in opposite directions shows two rays extending outward, with the middle left unshaded.
On a number line, an open circle means the endpoint is not included (< or >) and a closed circle means it is included (≤ or ≥).
An AND solution such as x > 2 and x < 5 is written as 2 < x < 5, and in interval notation as (2, 5).
Interval notation uses parentheses for excluded endpoints and square brackets for included endpoints; infinity always gets a parenthesis. Example: −1 ≤ x < 4 is [−1, 4).
An OR solution such as x < −1 or x ≥ 3 is written in interval notation as (−∞, −1) ∪ [3, ∞), where ∪ means union.
An OR solution cannot be written as one combined inequality like a < x < b; it needs two separate inequalities.
An AND with no overlap, such as x < 2 and x > 5, has no solution; the solution set is the empty set, written ∅ or { }.
An OR whose rays cover the whole number line, such as x < 5 or x > 2, has all real numbers as solutions, written (−∞, ∞).
A three-part inequality like −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 is solved by applying each operation to all three parts: subtract 1 to get −4 < 2x ≤ 6, divide by 2 to get −2 < x ≤ 3.
Dividing a three-part inequality by a negative flips both signs and the order: −6 ≤ −3x < 9 becomes 2 ≥ x > −3, which is written −3 < x ≤ 2.

misconceptions: Treating AND like OR (taking everything shaded by either part).
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
Flipping the sign when subtracting a negative or adding.
Writing an OR solution as a single chain like 5 < x < 2, which is not valid.
Using brackets with infinity; infinity always takes a parenthesis.
Mixing up open and closed circles or parentheses and brackets for < versus ≤.
Thinking an AND with no overlap is an error rather than the empty set.
Thinking 'or' means exactly one part is true; in math it includes both being true.
Writing a three-part inequality in the wrong order, such as 5 < x < 2.

plans.approach: A typical 9th-grade learner needs concrete graph reading before formal interval language, so the lesson moves from a worked anatomy of one graph to guided practice and a misconception trap, then consolidates with a memory anchor. Each feature (intercepts, increase/decrease, extrema, symmetry) is taught once, practiced, and retrieved later.
coverage: Identify x-intercepts (zeros) and y-intercept from a graph and from a table
State intervals of increase and decrease using interval notation on x
Identify local/absolute maxima and minima and their coordinates
Recognize symmetry (about the y-axis, about the origin) from a graph or table
Use correct language: 'increases on the interval', 'maximum value of f is', 'symmetric about'
Distinguish intercepts (points) from zeros (input values) and read features from tables when no graph is given
Avoid common errors: reading intervals on the y-axis, calling a point a maximum value, confusing x- and y-intercepts

data.title: Anatomy of a function graph
data.caption: Tap or focus each labeled part to see what it tells you. The graph shows f(x) = -x^2 + 4x, a parabola that opens downward.

labels.pickerAria: Choose a feature of the graph
labels.emptyHint: Select a labeled part of the graph.

parts.label: x-intercepts (zeros)
parts.role: Where the graph meets the x-axis
parts.description: An x-intercept is a point (x, 0) where the output is 0. The input in that point is called a zero of the function. This graph has two x-intercepts: (0, 0) and (4, 0), so its zeros are x = 0 and x = 4.
parts.example: f(0) = 0 and f(4) = 0, so the zeros are 0 and 4.

parts.label: y-intercept
parts.role: Where the graph meets the y-axis
parts.description: The y-intercept is the point (0, f(0)) — the output when the input is 0. Here the graph crosses the y-axis at (0, 0).

parts.label: Interval of increase
parts.role: Where the graph goes up left to right
parts.description: The function increases on an interval of x-values where the outputs get larger as x gets larger. State it on the x-axis, never the y-axis. On the part of the graph shown (from x = 0 to x = 4), f increases on the interval (0, 2).
parts.example: Increases on (0, 2): as x goes from 0 to 2, f(x) rises from 0 to 4.

parts.label: Interval of decrease
parts.role: Where the graph goes down left to right
parts.description: The function decreases on an interval of x-values where the outputs get smaller as x gets larger. On the part of the graph shown (from x = 0 to x = 4), f decreases on the interval (2, 4).
parts.example: Decreases on (2, 4): as x goes from 2 to 4, f(x) falls from 4 to 0.

parts.label: Maximum
parts.role: The highest point on the graph
parts.description: The maximum point is (2, 4). The maximum value of f is 4 — the output, not the input. Say 'the maximum value of f is 4', not 'the maximum is 2'.
parts.example: f(2) = -(2)^2 + 4(2) = -4 + 8 = 4, so the maximum value of f is 4.

parts.label: Symmetry
parts.description: This parabola is symmetric about the vertical line x = 2. Points the same distance left and right of x = 2 have equal outputs: f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 3.
parts.example: f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 3, so the graph is symmetric about x = 2.

A point on a graph is written (x, y), with the input first and the output second.

blocks.purpose: Confront the top misconceptions: reading intervals on the y-axis, calling a point 'the maximum' instead of its y-value, and mixing up x- and y-intercepts.

data.flagIntro: Each trap below comes from a habit that feels right. Read the wrong and right versions side by side.

cautions.title: Intervals live on the x-axis
cautions.detail: An interval of increase or decrease is a range of inputs, so read it from the x-axis. Reading the y-values gives you the outputs, not the interval.
cautions.exampleNote: On the part of the graph shown, for f(x) = -x^2 + 4x the outputs run from 0 to 4, but the inputs where it rises run from 0 to 2.

cautions.title: A point is not a value
cautions.detail: The maximum point is a location (x, y). The maximum value is the y-coordinate alone. Mixing them up swaps the input for the output.
cautions.rightExample: The maximum value of f is 4, at x = 2
cautions.exampleNote: The point is (2, 4); the value is 4.

cautions.title: x-intercepts and the y-intercept are found differently
cautions.detail: The x-intercept has y = 0 and the y-intercept has x = 0. A graph can have several x-intercepts but at most one y-intercept. Sometimes a point can be both.
cautions.rightExample: An x-intercept is (4, 0); the y-intercept is (0, 0)
cautions.exampleNote: Check which coordinate is 0 before you name the intercept. Here (0, 0) is both an x-intercept and the y-intercept.

data.footerNote: Before you write an answer, ask: am I naming an input, an output, or a point?

data.question: A graph of f has its highest point at (2, 4). Which statement is correct?
data.context: The graph of f(x) = -x^2 + 4x rises from (0, 0) to (2, 4), then falls back to (4, 0).
choices: The maximum value of f is 4, and f increases on the interval (0, 2).

The maximum value of f is 4, and f increases on the interval (0, 4).
The maximum value of f is 2, and f increases on the interval (0, 2).
data.commonErrorLabel: Reading the interval on y and calling the input the maximum

trapReasons.1: The 2 is the x-coordinate of the peak, and 0 to 4 is the range of outputs — both are the wrong axis.
trapReasons.2: The value 4 is right, but 0 to 4 is the range of y-values, not the x-values where the graph rises.
trapReasons.3: The interval is right, but 2 is the input at the peak, not the maximum value.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Learners often grab the biggest numbers they see. But the maximum value is the output at the peak, and the interval of increase is a stretch of inputs. The 2 and the 4 play different roles.
data.correctReasoning: The peak is (2, 4). The maximum value of f is the y-coordinate, 4. The graph rises from x = 0 to x = 2, so f increases on the interval (0, 2).
data.recoveryTip: Say the sentence out loud with the axis named: 'increases on the x-interval from 0 to 2' and 'the maximum value of f is 4'. If the axis is not named, you probably grabbed the wrong number.

claims.truth: -x^2+4x = -x(x-4) = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 4.

claims.claim: f(0) = 0 and f(4) = 0, so the zeros are 0 and 4.
The y-intercept is the point (0, f(0)) — the output when the input is 0. Here the graph crosses the y-axis at (0, 0).
f(0) = -(0)^2 + 4(0) = 0, so the y-intercept is (0, 0).
The function increases on an interval of x-values where the outputs get larger as x gets larger. State it on the x-axis, never the y-axis.
On the part of the graph shown (from x = 0 to x = 4), f increases on the interval (0, 2).
claims.truth: True because it is limited to the part shown. The full parabola also rises for x < 0.

claims.claim: Increases on (0, 2): as x goes from 0 to 2, f(x) rises from 0 to 4.
The function decreases on an interval of x-values where the outputs get smaller as x gets larger. On the part of the graph shown (from x = 0 to x = 4), f decreases on the interval (2, 4).
Decreases on (2, 4): as x goes from 2 to 4, f(x) falls from 4 to 0.
The maximum point is (2, 4). The maximum value of f is 4 — the output, not the input. Say 'the maximum value of f is 4', not 'the maximum is 2'.
claims.truth: Vertex is at x = -b/(2a) = 2, and f(2) = 4.

claims.claim: f(2) = -(2)^2 + 4(2) = -4 + 8 = 4, so the maximum value of f is 4.
This parabola is symmetric about the vertical line x = 2. Points the same distance left and right of x = 2 have equal outputs: f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 3.
f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 3, so the graph is symmetric about x = 2.
claims.truth: The arithmetic is right and the symmetry is true. Two matching points illustrate symmetry but do not prove it. Consider 'for example, f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 3, which fits symmetry about x = 2'.

claims.claim: Diagram: curve through (0,0), peak (2,4), (4,0); labels 'increasing on (0, 2)', 'decreasing on (2, 4)', 'line of symmetry x = 2', 'maximum (2, 4)'
claims.truth: The Bezier path peaks at (160,110) and the points are placed at x = 60, 160, 260, which matches the labels.

claims.claim: An interval of increase or decrease is a range of inputs, so read it from the x-axis. Reading the y-values gives you the outputs, not the interval.
Wrong: 'Increases on (0, 4)'; right: 'Increases on (0, 2)'. On the part of the graph shown, for f(x) = -x^2 + 4x the outputs run from 0 to 4, but the inputs where it rises run from 0 to 2.
The maximum point is a location (x, y). The maximum value is the y-coordinate alone. Mixing them up swaps the input for the output.
Wrong: 'The maximum is 2'; right: 'The maximum value of f is 4, at x = 2'. The point is (2, 4); the value is 4.
The x-intercept has y = 0 and the y-intercept has x = 0.
A graph can have several x-intercepts but at most one y-intercept. Sometimes a point can be both.
claims.truth: True for graphs of functions, which is the context here. Only the origin can be both.

claims.claim: Wrong: 'The y-intercept is (4, 0)'; right: 'An x-intercept is (4, 0); the y-intercept is (0, 0)'. Here (0, 0) is both an x-intercept and the y-intercept.
Each trap below comes from a habit that feels right. / Three common traps
claims.truth: Framing about common learner mistakes. It is reasonable as written.

claims.claim: The graph of g(x) = -(x - 3)^2 + 4, a downward parabola with vertex at (3, 4).
Diagram label (1, 0) and (5, 0) as x-intercepts
claims.truth: -(x-3)^2+4 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = 5.

claims.claim: Hotspot B 'y-intercept' at the green point on the y-axis (pixel 80, 340), which is about (0, 1.75) on the grid
claims.truth: g(0) = -(0-3)^2 + 4 = -5, so the real y-intercept is (0, -5). The drawn curve only spans x = 1 to 5, so it never reaches the y-axis. The green point at height 1.75 is not on the graph, and the figure has no y-intercept. Remove this distractor. Alternatively, extend the curve to the y-axis, put the point at (0, -5) with a rescaled grid, and label it (0, -5).

claims.claim: Click the maximum point of the graphed function. (Answer: hotspot C, the peak at (3, 4))
claims.truth: The peak is at pixel (500,160), which is (3,4) on the scale. Hotspot C is the only correct choice.

claims.claim: The highest point on the graph is (3, 4). The maximum value of g is 4, and it happens at x = 3.
The maximum point is the highest point on the curve, not a place where the graph crosses an axis. Look for the peak.
The peak is at (3, 4), so the maximum point is (3, 4) and the maximum value of g is 4.
The graph of f(x) = -x^2 + 4x rises from (0, 0) to (2, 4), then falls back to (4, 0).
Correct answer: 'The maximum value of f is 4, and f increases on the interval (0, 2).'
claims.truth: This is the only choice with max value 4 and an interval of increase that is true on the part shown. The other three each contain a false part.

claims.claim: Distractor 1: 'The 2 is the x-coordinate of the peak, and 0 to 4 is the range of outputs — both are the wrong axis.'
Distractor 2: 'The value 4 is right, but 0 to 4 is the range of y-values, not the x-values where the graph rises.'
Distractor 3: 'The interval is right, but 2 is the input at the peak, not the maximum value.'
Learners often grab the biggest numbers they see.
claims.truth: This is hedged with 'often' and is a teaching observation, not a measured statistic. It is acceptable as written.

claims.claim: The peak is (2, 4). The maximum value of f is the y-coordinate, 4. The graph rises from x = 0 to x = 2, so f increases on the interval (0, 2).
Say the sentence out loud with the axis named... If the axis is not named, you probably grabbed the wrong number.
X in, Y out; intervals live on x; a max is a y, a point is a pair.
The input comes first in every point; an interval is written with x-values.
The output f(x) is the second coordinate and the value of the function.
Increase and decrease are stated with x-values, never y-values.
The maximum value is the output at the peak; the peak itself is a point (x, y).
The chant names the axis for each feature, so a quick recital catches common slips.
claims.truth: This is a claim about how well the chant works, and no evidence is given for it. The chant also does not cover every feature, such as intercepts and symmetry. Reword to something like: 'The chant reminds you which axis each idea belongs to, which can help you catch common slips.'

claims.claim: A graph of f rises from the point (1, 2) to the point (5, 10), then falls after x = 5. On what interval is f increasing on the part of the graph described?
claims.truth: The interval is x = 1 to x = 5, and the phrase 'on the part described' avoids any claim about x < 1.

claims.claim: answer: "(1, 5)"
claims.truth: (1, 5) is correct, but the rationale says [1, 5] is also acceptable. The type_in answer key lists only '(1, 5)', so a correct '[1, 5]' could be marked wrong. Add '[1, 5]' (and variants with spaces or 'x = 1 to 5') as accepted answers, or change the prompt to ask for open interval notation.

claims.claim: The graph rises between x = 1 and x = 5, so the interval of increase on the described part is (1, 5) or the closed [1, 5].
claims.truth: Both open and closed endpoints are used for intervals of increase in Algebra 1.

claims.claim: Click the maximum point of the graphed function.
claims.truth: Doable for a 14-year-old. There is one clear maximum, the vertex.

claims.claim: The graph of g(x) = -(x - 3)^2 + 4, a downward parabola with vertex at (3, 4).
claims.truth: The leading coefficient is negative, so the parabola opens downward. The vertex form -(x-3)^2+4 gives the vertex (3, 4).

claims.claim: (1, 0) and (5, 0) labelled as the x-intercepts
claims.truth: Setting g(x)=0 gives (x-3)^2=4, so x=1 or x=5. Both are correct.

claims.claim: Diagram geometry: the points at pixels (220,480), (780,480) and (500,160) and the curve 'M 220 480 Q 500 -160 780 480' match (1,0), (5,0) and (3,4)
claims.truth: The scale is 140 px per x-unit with the origin at x=80, and 80 px per y-unit with the axis at y=480. The points map correctly. The Bezier curve's midpoint is at (500,160), and its end tangents match the parabola's slopes, so the curve is the parabola. The labels agree with the hotspots.

claims.claim: The caption presents the drawing as 'The graph of g(x) = -(x - 3)^2 + 4' (the curve is drawn only from x = 1 to x = 5)
claims.truth: The real graph of g continues downward past both intercepts. The drawing shows only part of it, which could mislead a learner. The maximum is still correct. Reword to 'part of the graph of g' or extend the curve with arrows.

claims.claim: The highest point on the graph is (3, 4). The maximum value of g is 4, and it happens at x = 3.
claims.truth: g(3)=4 and g(x) ≤ 4 for all x.

claims.claim: The maximum point is the highest point on the curve, not a place where the graph crosses an axis. Look for the peak.
claims.truth: Correct. The x-intercepts are where the graph crosses the x-axis, and the maximum is the peak.

claims.claim: The peak is at (3, 4), so the maximum point is (3, 4) and the maximum value of g is 4.
claims.truth: Correct.

claims.claim: Hotspot answerId 'max' is the only correct hotspot (others: x-intercept at (1,0), other x-intercept at (5,0))
claims.truth: Only the vertex (500,160) is the maximum. The two intercept hotspots are wrong. The tags skip 'B' (A, C, D), which is harmless.

claims.claim: X in, Y out; intervals live on x; a max is a y, a point is a pair.
claims.truth: Each phrase is mathematically correct. It is labelled mnemonicType 'rhyme' but it does not really rhyme, which is a style point only.

claims.claim: The input comes first in every point; an interval is written with x-values.
claims.truth: In an ordered pair (x, y) the input x comes first. Intervals of increase and decrease are written in x-values.

claims.claim: The output f(x) is the second coordinate and the value of the function.
claims.truth: Correct.

claims.claim: Increase and decrease are stated with x-values, never y-values.
claims.truth: Intervals of increase and decrease are intervals of the input x, which is the standard convention.

claims.claim: The maximum value is the output at the peak; the peak itself is a point (x, y).
claims.truth: Correct. The maximum value is a y-value, and the maximum point is (x, y).

claims.claim: The chant reminds you which axis each idea belongs to, which can help you catch common slips.
claims.truth: It is hedged ('can help'), so it is acceptable as a labelled opinion.

claims.claim: A graph of f rises from the point (1, 2) to the point (5, 10), then falls after x = 5. On what interval is f increasing on the part of the graph described? Give your answer in interval notation using x-values.
claims.truth: The question is clear and solvable. It restricts the answer to 'the part described', which removes any ambiguity about the rest of f.

claims.claim: answer: (1, 5)
claims.truth: (1, 5) is correct, but [1, 5] is equally correct, and the rationale itself says so. A type_in check with only '(1, 5)' as its key would mark a correct [1, 5] wrong. Either accept both forms (for example '(1, 5)' and '[1, 5]'), or reword the prompt to ask for an open interval.

claims.claim: The graph rises between x = 1 and x = 5, so the interval of increase on the described part is (1, 5) or the closed [1, 5].
claims.truth: Textbooks differ: some write increasing on open intervals and others include the endpoints. The rationale does say both are acceptable, so it is labelled. It is consistent with the question, but the answer key must match it.

claims.claim: Part of the graph of g(x) = -(x - 3)^2 + 4, shown between its x-intercepts.
claims.truth: Setting g(x)=0 gives (x-3)^2=4, so x=1 or x=5. The drawn arc runs from x=1 to x=5. Converting the Bézier path to the grid (140 px per x-unit, 80 px per y-unit) gives, for example, g(2)=3, which matches the drawing.

claims.claim: The parabola opens downward with vertex at (3, 4).
claims.truth: The leading coefficient is -1, so the parabola opens downward. In vertex form the vertex is (3, 4).

claims.claim: (1, 0) and (5, 0) labelled as the x-intercepts, and (3, 4) labelled at the peak
claims.truth: g(1)=0, g(5)=0 and g(3)=4. The pixel positions (220,480), (780,480) and (500,160) match these points on the grid, and the Bézier peak is at y=160. The hotspot positions match the circles.

claims.claim: Click the maximum point of the graphed function.
claims.truth: Safe and doable. The only correct hotspot is B (id 'max'), the vertex (3, 4). The other two hotspots are the x-intercepts, so they are wrong.

claims.claim: The highest point on the graph is (3, 4). The maximum value of g is 4, and it happens at x = 3.
claims.truth: g(x) = 4 - (x-3)^2 ≤ 4, with equality only at x=3.

claims.claim: The maximum point is the highest point on the curve, not a place where the graph crosses an axis. Look for the peak.
claims.truth: The maximum point is the highest point on the graph. On this graph it is the peak, not an intercept.

claims.claim: The peak is at (3, 4), so the maximum point is (3, 4) and the maximum value of g is 4.
claims.truth: Correct.

claims.claim: A graph of f rises from the point (1, 2) to the point (5, 10), then falls after x = 5.
claims.truth: This is a consistent description of a graph, with a peak at (5, 10). 'On the part of the graph described' limits the question to this stretch.

claims.claim: On what interval is f increasing on the part of the graph described? Give your answer in interval notation using x-values. (Either open or closed brackets are accepted.)
claims.truth: The question has one answer, x from 1 to 5, and it asks for x-values. The type_in key must accept (1, 5) and [1, 5]. Other forms such as 1<x<5 are not interval notation, so they are not required.

claims.claim: The graph climbs from x = 1 to x = 5, so the interval of increase is (1, 5).
claims.truth: f increases as x goes from 1 to 5, so the interval of increase is (1, 5). Intervals of increase are given in x-values.

claims.claim: Some textbooks include the endpoints and write [1, 5], so both are accepted.
claims.truth: Textbooks differ: some use open intervals and some use closed ones. The wording 'some textbooks' labels this as a convention, and the answer key accepts both.
