plans.approach: A typical learner needs a concrete anchor before abstract form-juggling, so the lesson starts with a real choice between forms, then teaches each form in short chunks with a worked conversion, and finishes with retrieval practice on the sign and fraction traps. Games and interactive checks keep the 14-year-old practicing actively rather than reading passively.
coverage: Point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and what each part means
Slope-intercept form y = mx + b and what m and b represent
Standard form Ax + By = C with integer A, B, C and A ≥ 0 convention
Converting point-slope to slope-intercept by distributing and solving for y
Converting slope-intercept or point-slope to standard form by clearing fractions and rearranging
Choosing the form that fits the given information (a point and slope → point-slope; slope and intercept → slope-intercept; two intercepts or integer constraints
Common error: sign mistakes when subtracting negative coordinates in point-slope
Common error: forgetting to clear fractions or flip signs when rearranging to standard form
Recognizing that all three forms describe the same line

blocks.purpose: Present two plausible ways to record a line (a point and slope vs. two intercepts) so the learner feels why different forms exist before any formula appears.

data.prompt: Two students are recording the same line. Which note would you rather work from?
data.context: A line passes through the point (2, 5) and has a slope of 3. It also crosses the y-axis at -1 and the x-axis at 1/3. Both notes below describe that exact same line.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: "Slope 3, goes through (2, 5)"
leftChoice.body: You know the steepness and one point the line passes through. Nothing else is written down.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: "Crosses y at -1, crosses x at 1/3"
rightChoice.body: You know exactly where the line cuts both axes, but no slope is written down.

data.footerNote: Neither note is wrong. The question is which one makes the next step easier, and that depends on what you were given.

blocks.purpose: Anchor point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with a one-sentence definition and the prerequisite ideas (slope, a point on the line, coordinates).

data.anchor: Point-slope form is y - y1 = m(x - x1), where m is the slope and (x1, y1) is any point on the line.
prerequisites: Slope m is rise over run: the change in y divided by the change in x between any two points on the line.
A point on the line is an ordered pair (x1, y1) whose coordinates make the equation true.
Subtracting a negative coordinate means adding: y - (-3) is the same as y + 3.
The variables x and y stay as letters; only m, x1, and y1 get replaced by numbers.

blocks.purpose: Place point-slope, slope-intercept, and standard forms side by side so the learner sees what each reveals and when to pick it.

data.title: Three Forms, Three Jobs
data.subtitle: Same line every time. What changes is which fact the equation puts in front of you.

items.label: Point-slope: y - y1 = m(x - x1)
items.text: Shows the slope and one point immediately. Best when a problem hands you a slope and a point.
items.example: y - 5 = 3(x - 2) shows slope 3 through (2, 5).

items.label: Slope-intercept: y = mx + b
items.text: Shows the slope and the y-intercept. Best when you are given a slope and where the line crosses the y-axis, or when you need to graph fast.
items.example: y = 3x - 1 shows slope 3 and y-intercept -1.

items.label: Standard: Ax + By = C
items.text: Puts both variables on one side with integer coefficients. Standard form is often a handy choice when a problem asks for whole-number coefficients, and it can also be built from two intercepts.
items.example: 3x - y = 1, which is the same line again.

items.label: Not different lines
items.text: Converting a form never changes the line. If a point worked before the conversion, it still works after.
items.example: (2, 5) satisfies all three equations above.

items.label: Not a free choice in every problem
items.text: The information you are given usually points to one form as the fastest start.
items.example: Given slope and y-intercept, starting in point-slope adds work.

items.label: Not allowed to keep fractions in standard form
items.text: Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should not be negative.
items.example: (1/2)x + y = 3 must become x + 2y = 6.

data.footnote: Pick the form that matches what you were handed, then convert only if the question asks for a different one.

blocks.purpose: Map the conversion decision path: given information → which form to start with → the steps to reach the requested form.

data.title: Which Form Do I Start With?
data.subtitle: Follow the given information to a starting form, then convert if needed.

nodes.label: Two intercepts or integer coefficients required?
Start in point-slope
nodes.detail: y - y1 = m(x - x1)

nodes.detail: y = mx + b

legend.label: Rectangle: the form you start writing in

data.footer: Converting is always allowed. It just costs steps, so start where the information already lives.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the worked conversion procedure: distribute m, solve for y for slope-intercept, or clear fractions and rearrange for standard form.

data.title: The Conversion Procedure
data.subtitle: Worked on the line through (2, 5) with slope 3, which is y - 5 = 3(x - 2).

steps.label: Step 1: Distribute the slope
steps.text: Multiply m by each term inside the parentheses: y - 5 = 3x - 6.
steps.detail: Watch the sign: 3 times -2 is -6, not +6.

steps.label: Step 2: Solve for y to reach slope-intercept
steps.text: Add 5 to both sides: y = 3x - 1.
steps.detail: Now the slope 3 and the y-intercept -1 are both visible.

steps.label: Step 3: Move the x-term to reach standard form
steps.text: From y = 3x - 1, subtract 3x from both sides: -3x + y = -1.
steps.detail: Both variables now sit on the left side.

steps.label: Step 4: Clear fractions
steps.text: If any coefficient is a fraction, multiply every term by the common denominator.
steps.detail: Example: y = (1/2)x + 3 becomes 2y = x + 6, then -x + 2y = 6.

steps.label: Step 5: Make A positive
steps.text: If the x-coefficient is negative, multiply the whole equation by -1.
steps.detail: -3x + y = -1 becomes 3x - y = 1. Same line, A = 3.

steps.label: Step 6: Check with a point
steps.text: Substitute a point you know is on the line into the final equation.

blocks.purpose: Flag the two classic errors — mishandling y − (−3) as y − 3, and leaving fractions or a negative leading coefficient in standard form.

data.flagIntro: These are common mistakes on this topic.

cautions.title: Subtracting a negative coordinate
cautions.detail: The formula already contains a minus sign. When y1 is negative, subtracting a negative gives a plus. y - (-3) simplifies to y + 3.

cautions.title: Leaving fractions or a negative A in standard form
cautions.detail: Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should be zero or positive. Multiply through by the denominator to clear fractions, then multiply by -1 if the x-term is negative.
cautions.exampleNote: Multiply the first by 3; multiply the second by -1.

cautions.title: Not every equation with x and y is standard form
cautions.detail: Standard form requires both variables on the same side with integer coefficients and a constant alone on the other side. An equation solved for y is slope-intercept, not standard.

data.footerNote: Before you turn in an answer, ask two questions: did I handle every negative sign, and are all my coefficients integers with A positive?

blocks.purpose: Have the learner drag the correct pieces (m, x₁, y₁, b, A, B, C) into labeled slots of each form to check structural understanding.

data.subtitle: Point-slope, slope-intercept, and standard form

checks.prompt: The line y - 6 = -2(x + 3) is written in point-slope form. What are m, x1, and y1?
checks.rationale: Rewrite x + 3 as x - (-3) so the equation matches y - y1 = m(x - x1); then m = -2, x1 = -3, and y1 = 6.
checks.hint: The formula has a minus in front of x1. What number, subtracted from x, gives x + 3?
checks.focus: Identify m, x₁, y₁ from a point-slope equation, including a negative coordinate

checks.prompt: A line has slope -4 and passes through the point (7, 2). Which form is the fastest place to start writing its equation?
checks.answer: Point-slope form, because you are given a slope and one point
checks.rationale: The given information is exactly m and one point, which are the two ingredients of y - y1 = m(x - x1).
checks.hint: Match the facts you were handed to the parts each form displays.
choices: Point-slope form, because you are given a slope and one point
Slope-intercept form, because you are given a slope and the y-intercept
Standard form, because you are given two intercepts
Standard form, because the coefficients must be integers

checks.prompt: A student writes the point-slope equation of the line through (5, -2) with slope 4 as y - 2 = 4(x - 5). What went wrong?
checks.answer: The y-coordinate was substituted wrong: y - (-2) should become y + 2
checks.rationale: Substituting y1 = -2 into y - y1 gives y - (-2), which simplifies to y + 2, so the correct equation is y + 2 = 4(x - 5).
checks.hint: Put -2 into the y1 slot of y - y1 and simplify the double sign.
choices: The y-coordinate was substituted wrong: y - (-2) should become y + 2
The slope should have been written as -4
The x-coordinate was substituted wrong: x - 5 should become x + 5
Nothing went wrong; the equation is correct

checks.prompt: Rewrite y = (2/3)x - 4 in standard form with integer coefficients and A positive. Give just the equation.
checks.rationale: Multiplying every term by 3 gives 3y = 2x - 12; moving the x-term left gives -2x + 3y = -12, and multiplying by -1 gives 2x - 3y = 12.
checks.hint: Clear the fraction with a factor of 3, then make the x-term positive.

dropped_checks.why: false: "answer: "3x - 2"" → The algebra is right but the answer key is not an equation. y - 4 = 3(x - 2) gives y = 3x - 2, so the accepted answer must include "y =" (e.g., "y = 3x - 2"); as written, a student typing the correct equation would be marked wrong, and the key itself violates the prompt's "give just the equation."

claims.claim: A line passes through the point (2, 5) and has a slope of 3. It also crosses the y-axis at -1 and the x-axis at 1/3.
Both notes below describe that exact same line.
claims.truth: Option A gives y = 3x - 1. Option B gives intercepts (0, -1) and (1/3, 0), which fit the same line.

claims.claim: Neither note is wrong. The question is which one makes the next step easier, and that depends on what you were given.
Point-slope form is y - y1 = m(x - x1), where m is the slope and (x1, y1) is any point on the line.
Slope m is rise over run: the change in y divided by the change in x between any two points on the line.
Subtracting a negative coordinate means adding: y - (-3) is the same as y + 3.
The variables x and y stay as letters; only m, x1, and y1 get replaced by numbers.
y - 5 = 3(x - 2) shows slope 3 through (2, 5). / y = 3x - 1 shows slope 3 and y-intercept -1. / 3x - y = 1, which is the same line again.
claims.truth: All three equations simplify to the same line. 3x - y = 1 is y = 3x - 1 rearranged.

claims.claim: (2, 5) satisfies all three equations above.
Standard: Ax + By = C ... Puts both variables on one side with integer coefficients.
Best when a problem gives you two intercepts or demands whole-number coefficients.
claims.truth: This is a teaching suggestion, not a rule. If both intercepts are given, the y-intercept is already known. Many students find the slope and use y = mx + b. Reword: 'Standard form is often a handy choice when a problem asks for whole-number coefficients, and it can also be built from two intercepts.'

claims.claim: Given slope and y-intercept, starting in point-slope adds work.
Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should not be negative.
claims.truth: This is the usual textbook convention (A is a non-negative integer). It matches the cheat sheet's 'A is zero or positive'.

claims.claim: (1/2)x + y = 3 must become x + 2y = 6.
claims.truth: Multiplying every term by 2 gives x + 2y = 6.

claims.claim: Edge: c3 'Two intercepts or integer coefficients required?' yes -> 'Start in standard form'
claims.truth: Starting in standard form is one reasonable choice but not the only one. With two intercepts you could find the slope and use y = mx + b. Reword the route as a suggestion, e.g. 'often easiest'.

claims.claim: Edge: c3 'no, use any point you have' -> 'Start in point-slope'
claims.truth: Point-slope form works with any point once you have the slope. If only two points are given, find the slope first.

claims.claim: Converting is always allowed. It just costs steps, so start where the information already lives.
Legend: 'Diamond: a question about the given information' / 'Rectangle: the form you start writing in'
claims.truth: The node 'Need a different form?' is a question, but it is a process rectangle and is not about the given information. It is also a conversion step, not a form you start in. Make it a diamond, or reword the legend, so the diagram matches its key.

claims.claim: Multiply m by each term inside the parentheses: y - 5 = 3x - 6.
Watch the sign: 3 times -2 is -6, not +6.
Add 5 to both sides: y = 3x - 1.
From y = 3x - 1, subtract 3x from both sides: -3x + y = -1.
If any coefficient is a fraction, multiply every term by the common denominator.
Example: y = (1/2)x + 3 becomes 2y = x + 6, then -x + 2y = 6.
If the x-coefficient is negative, multiply the whole equation by -1.
-3x + y = -1 becomes 3x - y = 1. Same line, A = 3.
Substitute a point you know is on the line into the final equation.
claims.truth: The instruction is fine, but the worked example below it is wrong.
The substitution is wrong. 3(2) - 1 = 5 is the check for y = 3x - 1, not for 3x - y = 1. Correct check: 3(2) - 5 = 6 - 5 = 1, so (2, 5) works in 3x - y = 1.

claims.claim: These two mistakes show up in almost every set of papers on this topic.
claims.truth: There is no source for this. Reword: 'These are common mistakes on this topic.' The block also shows three cautions, not two.

claims.claim: Two Traps That Cost the Most Points
claims.truth: No evidence ranks these as the costliest errors, and the block lists three cautions. Retitle, e.g. 'Common Traps'.

claims.claim: When y1 is negative, y - y1 turns into y plus a positive number. Keep the minus from the formula and the minus from the coordinate; they do not cancel into nothing.
claims.truth: The first sentence is correct. The second is confusing: the two minus signs combine into a plus (y - (-3) = y + 3). Reword: 'Subtracting a negative gives a plus.' The cheat sheet already says they combine into a plus.

claims.claim: Through (4, -3): y - 3 = m(x - 4) is wrong; y + 3 = m(x - 4) is right.
Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should be zero or positive. Multiply through by the denominator to clear fractions, then multiply by -1 if the x-term is negative.
(2/3)x + y = 4 and -5x + 2y = 8 ... rightExample 2x + 3y = 12 and 5x - 2y = -8 ... Multiply the first by 3; multiply the second by -1.
Standard form requires both variables on the same side with integer coefficients and a constant alone on the other side. An equation solved for y is slope-intercept, not standard.
y = 4x - 7 called standard form is wrong; 4x - y = 7 is standard form
In Ax + By = C, the letter A is the coefficient of... the x-term
claims.truth: A is the coefficient of x. The x-term is Ax. Reword the slot as 'A is the coefficient of...' with the chip 'x', or 'A is the number multiplying...' with the chip 'x'.

claims.claim: m stands for the slope; x1 and y1 are the coordinates of a point on the line; b is the y-intercept (the y-value when x = 0); C is the constant on the right.
Every chip is used exactly once.
claims.truth: There are 6 slots and 6 chips.

claims.claim: y - 4 = 2(x + 1) -> Point-Slope, with detail 'A minus sign before a group in parentheses'
claims.truth: The bin is correct (point (-1, 4), slope 2). The detail is wrong: the minus sign is before the 4, not before the parenthesised group. Reword: 'Slope times a group in parentheses'.

claims.claim: y = -3x + 8 -> Slope-Intercept; y = (1/2)x - 9 -> Slope-Intercept
5x + 2y = 10 -> Standard; x - 4y = 12 -> Standard ('A is 1, B is -4')
y + 7 = -1(x - 6) -> Point-Slope, 'Slope -1 written out'; y - 0 = 3(x - 0) -> Point-Slope, 'A point at the origin'
-2x + 6y = 18 -> Standard, 'A is negative, so it still needs fixing'
claims.truth: The shape is standard (Ax + By = C), but A is negative. Block 5 treats that as a mistake, so the detail's wording is needed to avoid confusion.

claims.claim: A, B, C are integers and A is zero or positive.
y - 5 = 3(x - 2) becomes y = 3x - 1.
y = (1/2)x + 3 becomes x - 2y = -6.
claims.truth: Multiplying by 2 gives 2y = x + 6, which rearranges to x - 2y = -6.

claims.claim: The formula's minus and the coordinate's minus combine into a plus.
(2/3)x + y = 4 becomes 2x + 3y = 12.
If the point satisfies both equations, the conversion is right.
claims.truth: One shared point does not prove two equations are the same line, because many lines pass through one point. A point check can show an error but cannot prove a conversion is right. Reword: 'If the point fails the new equation, the conversion is wrong. Check a second point to be more sure.'

claims.claim: Answer: m = -2, x1 = -3, y1 = 6 (rationale: rewrite x + 3 as x - (-3))
claims.truth: Only the first option is right. The other options have the wrong sign for x1, y1, or m.

claims.claim: Answer: Point-slope form, because you are given a slope and one point (other options wrongly cite a y-intercept or two intercepts)
claims.truth: The question gives only the slope -4 and the point (7, 2). The other three options are wrong.

claims.claim: Answer: The y-coordinate was substituted wrong: y - (-2) should become y + 2; correct equation y + 2 = 4(x - 5)
claims.truth: The other options are wrong: the slope 4 is right and x - 5 is right.

claims.claim: Answer: 2x - 3y = 12 (3y = 2x - 12; -2x + 3y = -12; multiply by -1)
claims.truth: The math is correct. The grader should also accept equivalent spellings such as '2x-3y=12'.

claims.claim: y - 5 = 3(x - 2) shows slope 3 through (2, 5).
Point-slope: Shows the slope and one point immediately. Best when a problem hands you a slope and a point.
y = 3x - 1 shows slope 3 and y-intercept -1.
claims.truth: y - 5 = 3x - 6, so y = 3x - 1. Correct.

claims.claim: Slope-intercept: Shows the slope and the y-intercept. Best when you are given a slope and where the line crosses the y-axis, or when you need to graph fast.

Standard: Puts both variables on one side with integer coefficients. Standard form is often a handy choice when a problem asks for whole-number coefficients, and it can also be built from two intercepts.
claims.truth: The text hedges with 'often'. Writing x/a + y/b = 1 and clearing the fractions gives standard form.

claims.claim: 3x - y = 1, which is the same line again.
claims.truth: From y = 3x - 1, subtracting 3x gives -3x + y = -1. Multiplying by -1 gives 3x - y = 1.

claims.claim: Converting a form never changes the line. If a point worked before the conversion, it still works after.
claims.truth: Valid algebra steps give equivalent equations, so they have the same solution set.

claims.claim: (2, 5) satisfies all three equations above.
claims.truth: 5 - 5 = 3(2 - 2) gives 0 = 0. 5 = 3(2) - 1 gives 5 = 5. 3(2) - 5 = 1 gives 1 = 1. All three hold.

claims.claim: The information you are given usually points to one form as the fastest start. / Given slope and y-intercept, starting in point-slope adds work.
claims.truth: With a slope and a y-intercept, y = mx + b can be written directly.

claims.claim: Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should not be negative.
claims.truth: This is the common textbook convention. It agrees with block 5 and block 8. Some books also ask for no common factor, which the lesson does not claim.

claims.claim: (1/2)x + y = 3 must become x + 2y = 6.
claims.truth: Multiplying by 2 gives x + 2y = 6.

claims.claim: Pick the form that matches what you were handed, then convert only if the question asks for a different one.

Edges: slope and one point -> point-slope; slope and y-intercept -> slope-intercept; two intercepts or integer coefficients required -> standard (yes, often easiest); otherwise point-slope ('no, use any point you have').
claims.truth: The branching is sound and matches block 2. The last branch assumes you can find the slope from the information given, for example from two points.

claims.claim: Converting is always allowed. It just costs steps, so start where the information already lives.
Distribute, solve for y, or clear fractions and rearrange
Step 1: Multiply m by each term inside the parentheses: y - 5 = 3x - 6. Watch the sign: 3 times -2 is -6, not +6.
Step 2: Add 5 to both sides: y = 3x - 1. Now the slope 3 and the y-intercept -1 are both visible.
Step 3: From y = 3x - 1, subtract 3x from both sides: -3x + y = -1. Both variables now sit on the left side.
Step 4: If any coefficient is a fraction, multiply every term by the common denominator. Example: y = (1/2)x + 3 becomes 2y = x + 6, then -x + 2y = 6.
claims.truth: Multiplying by 2 gives 2y = x + 6. Subtracting x gives -x + 2y = 6.

claims.claim: Step 5: If the x-coefficient is negative, multiply the whole equation by -1. -3x + y = -1 becomes 3x - y = 1. Same line, A = 3.
Step 6: Substitute a point you know is on the line into the final equation. 3(2) - 5 = 1, so (2, 5) works in 3x - y = 1.
When y1 is negative, subtracting a negative gives a plus. y - (-3) simplifies to y + 3.
Through (4, -3): y - 3 = m(x - 4) is wrong; y + 3 = m(x - 4) is right.
Standard form wants integers for A, B, and C, and A should be zero or positive. Multiply through by the denominator to clear fractions, then multiply by -1 if the x-term is negative.
claims.truth: This follows the usual convention and is consistent with block 2 and block 8.

claims.claim: Wrong: (2/3)x + y = 4 and -5x + 2y = 8. Right: 2x + 3y = 12 and 5x - 2y = -8. Multiply the first by 3; multiply the second by -1.
claims.truth: 3 times the first equation gives 2x + 3y = 12. -1 times the second gives 5x - 2y = -8.

claims.claim: Standard form requires both variables on the same side with integer coefficients and a constant alone on the other side. An equation solved for y is slope-intercept, not standard.
y = 4x - 7 called standard form is wrong; 4x - y = 7 is standard form. Same line, different form.
Before you turn in an answer, ask two questions: did I handle every negative sign, and are all my coefficients integers with A positive?
Slot answers: m = the slope; x1 = the x-coordinate of a point on the line; y1 = the y-coordinate of a point on the line; b = the y-intercept; A = the coefficient of x; C = the constant.
claims.truth: All six pairings are correct, and there are six slots and six chips, each used once. Strictly, b is also the y-coordinate of the point (0, b). The hints and the one-use rule keep the key unambiguous.

claims.claim: Chip notes: 'The y-value when x = 0.' / 'Rise over run.' / 'A must be an integer and not negative.' / 'An integer on the right side.' / 'Subtracted from y in the formula.' / 'Subtracted from x in the formula.'

Slot hints: the steepness of the line; first coordinate of the known point; second coordinate of the known point; where the line meets the y-axis; the variable written first; the number alone on the right.
All six placed correctly. You can now read every part of all three forms.
claims.truth: This is encouraging feedback, not a factual claim.

plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old learns best by seeing the slope rules concretely, then practising the two equation-writing procedures with immediate feedback. The lesson moves from the parallel/perpendicular slope rules to worked procedures to interactive practice, ending with a memory anchor and a misconception trap.
coverage: Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals (product = -1)
Vertical lines have undefined slope; horizontal lines have slope 0; vertical lines are parallel to vertical, horizontal to horizontal
Perpendicular slope is the flip-and-negate of the given slope (e.g., 2/3 → -3/2)
Write the equation of a line through a given point parallel to a given line: use same slope, then point-slope form
Write the equation of a line through a given point perpendicular to a given line: use negative reciprocal slope, then point-slope form
Convert the result to slope-intercept or standard form and verify the point satisfies the equation
Common error: using the reciprocal without negating, or negating without flipping, for perpendicular slopes
Common error: assuming any two lines with different slopes are perpendicular, or forgetting to check the product equals -1
Recognize parallel/perpendicular relationships from equations in standard form by comparing coefficients

blocks.purpose: Grab attention with a real-world fact about parallel and perpendicular lines (e.g., how city grids and skyscraper frames rely on exact slopes) to motivate the rules.

data.caption: The angle between every pair of perpendicular lines. City blocks in Manhattan's grid meet at this angle, and so do the steel frames of most skyscrapers.
data.context: Builders need exact right angles. The slope rule shows how to test for one with coordinates. Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to -1.
data.contrastLabel: What a tilted frame would do
data.contrastValue: a frame that is out of square can lean or put uneven stress on joints.

blocks.purpose: State the core anchor: parallel lines have equal slopes, perpendicular lines have negative reciprocal slopes (product = -1), with prerequisite bullets on slope, reciprocal, and negation.

data.ruleName: Slopes of Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
data.anchor: Parallel lines have equal slopes, and perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, so their product is -1.
prerequisites: Slope of a line through two points: m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).
Reciprocal of a fraction: flip it, so the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
Negating a number means changing its sign: the negative of 3/2 is -3/2.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side comparison of parallel vs perpendicular slope relationships, including vertical/horizontal special cases, so learners see the distinction clearly.

data.title: Parallel vs. Perpendicular: what each one requires
data.subtitle: Parallel needs exactly equal slopes. Perpendicular needs slopes that multiply to exactly -1.

items.label: Same slope
items.text: Two different lines with the same slope never meet.
items.example: y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 4 are parallel, both with slope 3.

items.label: Vertical and horizontal cases
items.text: All vertical lines are parallel to each other, and all horizontal lines are parallel to each other.
items.example: x = 2 and x = -5 are parallel; y = 7 and y = 0 are parallel.

items.label: Check with standard form
items.text: In Ax + By = C, the slope is -A/B, so equal A/B ratios mean parallel lines.
items.example: 2x + 5y = 10 and 4x + 10y = 3 both have slope -2/5.

items.label: Negative reciprocal slopes
items.text: Flip the slope and change its sign; the two slopes multiply to -1.
items.example: Slope 2/3 pairs with slope -3/2, since (2/3)(-3/2) = -1.

items.label: Vertical meets horizontal
items.text: A vertical line (undefined slope) is perpendicular to a horizontal line (slope 0).
items.example: x = 4 is perpendicular to y = -1.

items.label: Check with standard form
items.text: In Ax + By = C, perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1, which happens when the A/B ratios are negative reciprocals.
items.example: 3x + 4y = 8 has slope -3/4; 4x - 3y = 6 has slope 4/3, and their product is -1.

data.footnote: Different slopes alone do not make lines perpendicular. Always multiply the slopes and confirm the product is exactly -1.

blocks.purpose: Connect the abstract negative-reciprocal rule to an everyday physical image (e.g., a ramp and its perpendicular support) to make flip-and-negate intuitive.

data.rule: If a line has a nonzero slope m, a perpendicular line has slope -1/m.
data.ruleDetail: Flip the fraction and change its sign. When both slopes are defined, perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to -1.

analogies.because: A horizontal line and a vertical line always meet at 90 degrees. This is a special case of perpendicular lines, where the slopes cannot be multiplied because one is undefined.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the numbered procedure for writing an equation through a point parallel or perpendicular to a given line: find slope, apply rule, use point-slope, simplify.

data.title: Writing the equation of a parallel or perpendicular line
data.subtitle: Follow the same four steps every time; only step 2 changes.

steps.label: Step 1: Find the given slope
steps.text: Rewrite the given equation in slope-intercept form, y = mx + b, and read off m.
steps.detail: For example, 2x + 3y = 6 becomes y = -2/3 x + 2, so m = -2/3.

steps.label: Step 2: Apply the slope rule
steps.text: For parallel, keep the same slope. For perpendicular, flip it and change its sign.
steps.detail: From m = -2/3, parallel uses -2/3 and perpendicular uses 3/2.

steps.label: Step 3: Use point-slope form
steps.text: Substitute your new slope and the given point into y - y1 = m(x - x1).
steps.detail: Through (6, 1) with slope 3/2: y - 1 = 3/2 (x - 6).

steps.label: Step 4: Simplify and verify
steps.text: Solve for y to get slope-intercept form, then plug the point back in to check.
steps.detail: y = 3/2 x - 8, and 3/2(6) - 8 = 1, so the point (6, 1) checks out.

blocks.purpose: Let learners practise identifying the correct parallel or perpendicular slope from a given slope, with instant feedback on the flip-and-negate rule.

data.prompt: A line has slope 4/5. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?

byOption.a: Correct. Flip 4/5 to 5/4, then change the sign to get -5/4. Check: (4/5)(-5/4) = -1.
byOption.b: You flipped but did not change the sign. The product (4/5)(5/4) = 1, not -1.
byOption.c: You changed the sign but did not flip. The product (4/5)(-4/5) = -16/25, not -1.
byOption.d: That is the parallel slope, not the perpendicular one.

blocks.purpose: Have learners write the full equation of a line through a given point parallel or perpendicular to a given line, applying the procedure and checking their answer.

data.prompt: Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through the point (4, 1) that is parallel to y = 2x - 3.
data.context: Parallel means the same slope. The given line has slope 2. Use point-slope form with the point (4, 1), then simplify.
data.successMessage: Correct. Same slope 2, and 2(4) - 7 = 1, so the line passes through (4, 1).
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Keep the slope 2, substitute (4, 1) into y - 1 = 2(x - 4), and simplify.
data.explanation: y - 1 = 2(x - 4) becomes y - 1 = 2x - 8, so y = 2x - 7. Checking: 2(4) - 7 = 1.

blocks.purpose: Confront the #1 mistake: using the reciprocal without negating (or negating without flipping) for perpendicular slopes, and explain why intuition fails.

data.question: A line has slope 3/4. Which slope is perpendicular to it?
data.context: Perpendicular slopes must multiply to -1.
data.commonErrorLabel: Flipping without negating, or negating without flipping

trapReasons.1: You flipped 3/4 to 4/3 but forgot to change the sign. The product (3/4)(4/3) = 1, not -1.
trapReasons.2: You changed the sign but kept the fraction. The product (3/4)(-3/4) = -9/16, not -1.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: A common mistake is to do only half the rule.
data.correctReasoning: Flip 3/4 to get 4/3, then change the sign to get -4/3. Check the product: (3/4)(-4/3) = -12/12 = -1, so the lines are perpendicular.
data.recoveryTip: After you pick a perpendicular slope, multiply the two slopes. If the product is not exactly -1, you missed a step.

blocks.purpose: Provide a compact memory anchor (e.g., 'Same slope = parallel; flip-and-flip sign = perpendicular') to consolidate the rules for long-term retention.

data.title: Remember the slope rules
data.anchor: Parallel: keep the slope the same. Perpendicular: flip it, change its name.
data.subtitle: Two lines, two rules — one keeps the slope, one flips and changes its name.

expansions.phrase: Keep the slope exactly as it is.
Flip the fraction, then change its sign.
Multiply the slopes; perpendicular gives -1.

data.rationale: Pairing each relationship with one action can help you remember both steps of the perpendicular rule.

checks.prompt: A line has slope -3/7. What is the slope of a line parallel to it?
checks.rationale: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so the parallel line keeps the slope -3/7 unchanged.
checks.hint: Parallel means same slope. No flipping or sign change is needed.
checks.focus: Identify the slope of a line parallel to a given line

checks.prompt: A line has slope -2/5. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
checks.rationale: Flip -2/5 to -5/2, then change the sign to get 5/2. Check: (-2/5)(5/2) = -1.
checks.hint: Flip the fraction and change the sign, then multiply to confirm the product is -1.
checks.focus: Identify the slope of a line perpendicular to a given line (negative reciprocal)

checks.prompt: Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through (2, 5) that is parallel to y = 3x + 1.
checks.rationale: The parallel line keeps slope 3. Point-slope gives y - 5 = 3(x - 2), which simplifies to y = 3x - 1, and 3(2) - 1 = 5 checks the point.
checks.hint: Keep the slope 3, then substitute (2, 5) into y - y1 = m(x - x1) and simplify.
checks.focus: Write the equation of a line through a point parallel to a given line

checks.prompt: Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through (4, 2) that is perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.
checks.rationale: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal of 2, which is -1/2. Point-slope gives y - 2 = -1/2(x - 4), which simplifies to y = -1/2 x + 4, and -1/2(4) + 4 = 2 checks the point.
checks.hint: Flip 2 to 1/2 and change the sign to get -1/2, then use point-slope form with (4, 2).
checks.focus: Write the equation of a line through a point perpendicular to a given line

checks.prompt: A student says a line with slope 5/3 is perpendicular to a line with slope 3/5. What is wrong with this claim?
checks.answer: The slopes were flipped but not negated, so their product is 1, not -1.
checks.rationale: Perpendicular slopes must multiply to -1. Here (5/3)(3/5) = 1, so the student flipped without negating; the correct perpendicular slope is -3/5.
checks.hint: Multiply the two slopes. If the product is not -1, the lines are not perpendicular.
choices: The slopes were flipped but not negated, so their product is 1, not -1.

claims.claim: The angle between every pair of perpendicular lines [is 90°].
City blocks in Manhattan's grid meet at this angle, and so do the steel frames of most skyscrapers.
claims.truth: Manhattan's street grid is rectangular, so streets cross avenues at right angles. Broadway is a diagonal exception. Most skyscraper frames are rectilinear.

claims.claim: Builders cannot eyeball a right angle across a whole city block. They rely on slopes
claims.truth: Builders and surveyors lay out right angles with instruments such as theodolites and total stations, and with methods such as the 3-4-5 triangle. They do not mainly use slope products. Reword to something like: 'Builders need exact right angles. The slope rule shows how to test for one with coordinates.'

claims.claim: two lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to -1.
claims.truth: This holds only for non-vertical lines with nonzero slopes. A vertical line and a horizontal line are perpendicular, but the vertical line has no slope to multiply. Say: 'two non-vertical lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to -1.'

claims.claim: That one number keeps towers standing straight.
claims.truth: Exaggeration. A tower stays upright because of its structural design and construction, not because of the number -1. Remove it or reword it.

claims.claim: What a tilted frame would do: lean and crack
claims.truth: Vague and unsourced. A frame that is out of square does not necessarily crack. Reword, for example: 'a frame that is out of square can lean or put uneven stress on joints.'

claims.claim: Source: Geometry of city grids and structural engineering
claims.truth: This is a generic label, not a real citable source. Remove it or cite an actual source.

claims.claim: Parallel lines have equal slopes, and perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, so their product is -1.
claims.truth: True for non-vertical lines. Block 2 covers the vertical/horizontal case.

claims.claim: Slope of a line through two points: m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).
Reciprocal of a fraction: flip it, so the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
Negating a number means changing its sign: the negative of 3/2 is -3/2.
Same slope or opposite-reciprocal slope — nothing in between.
claims.truth: Ambiguous. Most pairs of lines are neither parallel nor perpendicular. The phrase could be read as saying every pair is one or the other. Reword: 'Parallel needs exactly equal slopes. Perpendicular needs slopes that multiply to exactly -1.'

claims.claim: Two different lines with the same slope never meet.
y = 3x + 1 and y = 3x - 4 are parallel, both with slope 3.
All vertical lines are parallel to each other, and all horizontal lines are parallel to each other.
claims.truth: This holds for distinct lines. Coincident lines are treated as parallel by some conventions.

claims.claim: x = 2 and x = -5 are parallel; y = 7 and y = 0 are parallel.
In Ax + By = C, the slope is -A/B, so equal A/B ratios mean parallel lines.
claims.truth: Requires B ≠ 0. Equal ratios also give the same line unless C differs in proportion.

claims.claim: 2x + 5y = 10 and 4x + 10y = 3 both have slope -2/5.
claims.truth: 5y = -2x + 10 gives slope -2/5. 10y = -4x + 3 gives slope -4/10 = -2/5. The lines are distinct, so they are parallel.

claims.claim: Flip the slope and change its sign; the two slopes multiply to -1.
Slope 2/3 pairs with slope -3/2, since (2/3)(-3/2) = -1.
A vertical line (undefined slope) is perpendicular to a horizontal line (slope 0). x = 4 is perpendicular to y = -1.
In Ax + By = C, perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1, which happens when the A/B ratios are negative reciprocals.
claims.truth: The slopes are -A1/B1 and -A2/B2. Their product is (A1/B1)(A2/B2), which equals -1 when the ratios are negative reciprocals.

claims.claim: 3x + 4y = 8 has slope -3/4; 4x - 3y = 6 has slope 4/3, and their product is -1.
Different slopes alone do not make lines perpendicular. Always multiply the slopes and confirm the product is exactly -1.
If one line has slope m, a perpendicular line has slope -1/m.
claims.truth: Requires m ≠ 0. Block 3's second analogy covers the horizontal/vertical case.

claims.claim: Flip the fraction and change its sign. The two slopes always multiply to -1.
A ramp rises 1 unit for every 4 units it runs, so its slope is 1/4. ... The perpendicular slope -4/1 = -4.
A ramp and the support that braces it meet at a right angle — that is the negative reciprocal at work.
claims.truth: The support is stated as perpendicular in this scenario. Real ramp braces are often vertical posts and are not generally perpendicular to the ramp. Reword it as a hypothetical: 'Imagine a support beam that meets a ramp at a right angle.'

claims.claim: The brace must drop steeply as it moves forward, exactly the flip-and-negate of the ramp's gentle rise.
claims.truth: A slope of -4 is steep and falling. This is consistent with the perpendicular rule.

claims.claim: The bottom edge of a frame is perfectly level, and the side edge rises straight up. Slope 0 paired with an undefined slope. A horizontal line and a vertical line always meet at 90 degrees, which is the special case of the perpendicular rule.
claims.truth: This is a special case where the product-of--1 rule does not apply, since one slope is undefined.

Many students remember only half the rule. Flipping alone gives a product of 1, and negating alone gives a product that is not -1.
claims.truth: The math is correct in general. The exception is slope ±1, where negating alone does give a product of -1. 'Many students' is a plausible teaching observation but has no source. Reword: 'A common mistake is to do only half the rule.'

claims.claim: Flip 3/4 to get 4/3, then change the sign to get -4/3. Check the product: (3/4)(-4/3) = -12/12 = -1
Parallel: same slope, no change. Perpendicular: flip and flip the sign.
claims.truth: The block is labelled as a rhyme, but 'change' and 'sign' do not rhyme. 'Flip and flip the sign' is also confusing, since flipping twice would undo the flip. Better wording: 'Parallel: keep the slope the same. Perpendicular: flip it, then change its name to negative.' Alternatively relabel it as a mnemonic phrase, not a rhyme, and write 'flip it and switch the sign.'

claims.claim: Keep the slope exactly as it is. / Flip the fraction, then change its sign. / Multiply the slopes; perpendicular gives -1.
The rhyme pairs each relationship with its one action, so you never apply half of the perpendicular rule.
claims.truth: Overclaim, and there is no rhyme. Reword: 'Pairing each relationship with one action can help you remember both steps of the perpendicular rule.'

claims.claim: A line has slope -3/7. A parallel line has slope -3/7 (answer); the other options 3/7, 7/3, -7/3 are wrong.
Flip -2/5 to -5/2, then change the sign to get 5/2. Check: (-2/5)(5/2) = -1. Answer 5/2.
claims.truth: 5/2 is the only correct option. -5/2 gives a product of 1, 2/5 gives -4/25... wait: (-2/5)(2/5) = -4/25, and -2/5 gives 4/25. None equals -1.

claims.claim: The parallel line keeps slope 3. Point-slope gives y - 5 = 3(x - 2), which simplifies to y = 3x - 1, and 3(2) - 1 = 5 checks the point. Answer: 3x - 1
claims.truth: Correct. The prompt asks for an equation, but the key is only '3x - 1'. The grader should also accept 'y = 3x - 1'.

claims.claim: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal of 2, which is -1/2. Point-slope gives y - 2 = -1/2(x - 4), which simplifies to y = -1/2 x + 4, and -1/2(4) + 4 = 2 checks the point. Answer: -1/2 x + 4
claims.truth: Correct. The grader should also accept 'y = -1/2 x + 4', '-x/2 + 4' and '-0.5x + 4'.

claims.claim: The slopes were flipped but not negated, so their product is 1, not -1. (Answer key). Perpendicular slopes must multiply to -1. Here (5/3)(3/5) = 1, so the student flipped without negating; the correct perpendicular slope is -3/5.
claims.truth: Correct. Options 2, 3 and 4 are wrong: the slopes are not equal and are reciprocals, and the lines are not parallel, so 'nothing is wrong' is false.

City blocks in Manhattan's grid meet at this angle, and so do the steel frames of most skyscrapers.
claims.truth: Manhattan's street grid (1811 Commissioners' Plan) has streets meeting avenues at right angles, and orthogonal steel framing is standard. Parts of lower Manhattan are not on the grid, but the claim says 'grid'.

But it is labelled a wheelchair ramp, and 1/4 (25%) is about three times steeper than the ADA maximum running slope of 1:12 (about 8.33%). A real wheelchair ramp could not have this slope. Use a different object (e.g. a steep roof, a skateboard ramp or a hillside) or change the numbers to something like 1/12.

claims.claim: The perpendicular slope -4/1 = -4.
The brace must drop steeply as it moves forward, exactly the flip-and-negate of the ramp's gentle rise.
claims.truth: Slope -4 is the correct negative reciprocal of 1/4, so a perpendicular brace does fall steeply. But a slope of 1/4 is not a 'gentle' rise for a wheelchair ramp (ADA max is 1:12). Reword to 'the ramp's shallow rise' using a non-wheelchair example.

claims.claim: If one line has slope m, a perpendicular line has slope -1/m.
claims.truth: Only true when m is not 0 (and the line is not vertical). If m = 0, -1/m is undefined; the perpendicular line is vertical. Honest wording: 'If a line has a nonzero slope m, a perpendicular line has slope -1/m.'

claims.claim: Flip the fraction and change its sign.
claims.truth: Correct way to get the negative reciprocal of a nonzero slope. E.g. 1/4 becomes -4/1 = -4.

claims.claim: The two slopes always multiply to -1.
claims.truth: Not always. A horizontal line (slope 0) is perpendicular to a vertical line (undefined slope), and those slopes cannot be multiplied. It also contradicts analogy 2 in the same block. Honest wording: 'When both slopes are defined, perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to -1.'

claims.claim: Imagine a support beam that meets a ramp at a right angle.
claims.truth: Safe and doable imagination prompt for age 14.

claims.claim: A ramp rises 1 unit for every 4 units it runs, so its slope is 1/4.
claims.truth: Slope = rise/run = 1/4.

claims.claim: A support beam meets the ramp at a right angle.
claims.truth: Premise of the scenario; consistent with the perpendicular slope -4. The 'support beam' is later called a 'brace', a minor wording mismatch.

claims.claim: The perpendicular slope -4/1 = -4.
claims.truth: The negative reciprocal of 1/4 is -4. Check: (1/4)(-4) = -1.

claims.claim: The brace must drop steeply as it moves forward, exactly the flip-and-negate of the ramp's shallow rise.
claims.truth: A line with slope -4 falls 4 units per 1 unit forward, so it is steep and descending, and it is perpendicular to the slope-1/4 ramp. This assumes the same scale on both axes.

claims.claim: The bottom edge of a frame is perfectly level, and the side edge rises straight up.
claims.truth: A level edge is horizontal and a straight-up edge is vertical.

claims.claim: Slope 0 paired with an undefined slope.
claims.truth: Horizontal lines have slope 0 and vertical lines have undefined slope.

claims.claim: A horizontal line and a vertical line always meet at 90 degrees, which is the special case of the perpendicular rule.
claims.truth: The 90-degree part is correct. Better wording: 'the special case where the -1/m rule does not apply', because 0 has no reciprocal.

claims.claim: If a line has a nonzero slope m, a perpendicular line has slope -1/m.
claims.truth: Correct. A line with defined, nonzero slope m is perpendicular to any line with slope -1/m.

claims.claim: Flip the fraction and change its sign.
claims.truth: This correctly describes taking the negative reciprocal.

claims.claim: When both slopes are defined, perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to -1.
claims.truth: Correct. m·(-1/m) = -1. If one slope is 0, the other is undefined, so the product rule does not apply. The text covers this case later.

claims.claim: Imagine a support beam that meets a ramp at a right angle.
claims.truth: This is a safe analogy prompt that suits 14-year-olds.

claims.claim: A ramp rises 1 unit for every 4 units it runs, so its slope is 1/4.
claims.truth: Slope = rise/run = 1/4.

claims.claim: A support beam meets the ramp at a right angle.
claims.truth: This is the scenario's premise. It is consistent with the perpendicular case.

claims.claim: The perpendicular slope -4/1 = -4.
claims.truth: The negative reciprocal of 1/4 is -4/1 = -4. Check: (1/4)(-4) = -1.

claims.claim: The brace must drop steeply as it moves forward, exactly the flip-and-negate of the ramp's shallow rise.
claims.truth: A slope of -4 means the line falls 4 units for each 1 unit forward, so it is steep and downward. The ramp's slope of 1/4 is shallow. This is the flip-and-negate of 1/4.

claims.claim: The bottom edge of a frame is perfectly level, and the side edge rises straight up.
claims.truth: A level edge is horizontal (slope 0). A side edge that rises straight up is vertical (undefined slope).

claims.claim: Slope 0 paired with an undefined slope.
claims.truth: Horizontal lines have slope 0 and vertical lines have undefined slope. They are perpendicular.

claims.claim: A horizontal line and a vertical line always meet at 90 degrees.
claims.truth: Correct. Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular.

claims.claim: This is a special case of perpendicular lines, where the slopes cannot be multiplied because one is undefined.
claims.truth: Correct. The product rule needs both slopes to be defined. The nonzero condition in the rule also excludes slope 0, whose -1/m would be undefined.

plans.approach: A typical learner needs a concrete hook, a clear discrete-vs-continuous contrast, worked domain/range writing, then hands-on sorting and graphing practice. The lesson closes with a misconception trap and a compact anchor so the discrete/continuous decision and domain restrictions stick.
coverage: Distinguish discrete data (countable, separate values) from continuous data (measurable, any value in an interval)
Decide which model fits a real situation: counting whole items → discrete; measuring amounts like time, height, temperature → continuous
Write domain and range for a discrete situation as a set of specific values
Write domain and range for a continuous situation using inequalities (e.g., 0 ≤ x ≤ 12)
Apply real-world restrictions: negatives often impossible (length, time, people), and context caps values (e.g., a tank holds at most 50 gallons)
Recognize that a graph of discrete data is separate points while continuous data is a connected line or curve
Avoid the common error of connecting dots for countable data or ignoring context limits on the domain

blocks.purpose: Pose two situations (counting tickets sold vs. measuring water in a tank) so the learner feels the pull between 'list the values' and 'any value in between' before any rule is named.

data.prompt: Two situations, two very different kinds of answer. Which one can you actually list value by value?
data.context: A school is selling tickets to a talent show, and the same school is filling a water tank for the show's finale. One answer comes as a list of separate numbers. The other comes as a range you can slide through.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: Tickets sold
leftChoice.body: The count of tickets sold so far: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. There is no such thing as 2.5 tickets sold.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: Water in the tank
rightChoice.body: The amount of water in the tank: it could be 12 gallons, or 12.3 gallons, or 12.37 gallons, depending on when you look.

data.footerNote: Both are real. The difference is whether the values come in separate steps or flow smoothly. Keep both pictures in mind.

blocks.purpose: Teach the core distinction side by side: discrete = countable separate values (tickets, people) vs. continuous = measurable values in an interval (time, height, water).

data.title: Discrete vs. Continuous Data
data.subtitle: Same idea, two different shapes of answer.

items.label: Countable
items.text: You get the values by counting whole items. There are gaps between one value and the next.
items.example: Number of students in a class: 24 or 25, never 24.6

items.label: Separate values
items.text: Only specific numbers make sense. The values between them have no meaning here.
items.example: Pages read: 7 pages or 8 pages, not 7.5 pages

items.label: Graph look
items.text: Plot separate dots. Do not connect them, because nothing happens between the dots.
items.example: Dots at x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with empty space between

items.label: Measurable
items.text: You get the values by measuring. Between any two values there is always another value.
items.example: Temperature: 71 degrees, 71.4 degrees, 71.42 degrees

items.label: Any value in an interval
items.text: Every number in the range is possible, including decimals and fractions.
items.example: Height of a plant: 12.5 cm is a real possible height

items.label: Graph look
items.text: Plot a connected line or curve, because the in-between values are real too.
items.example: A solid line from x = 0 to x = 12

data.footnote: Ask yourself: do I count it or do I measure it? Counting gives separate values; measuring gives a smooth interval.

blocks.purpose: Anchor the abstract idea to everyday objects: stairs (discrete steps you land on) vs. a ramp (continuous, every point in between).

data.rule: A discrete domain is a set of separate values. A continuous domain is an interval of values, written with inequalities.
data.ruleDetail: The situation decides which one you use, not the numbers themselves.
data.bridgeStatement: Stairs versus a ramp: same height change, different kinds of in-between.

analogies.everydayScene: You climb from the first floor to the second by landing on step 1, step 2, step 3, and so on. You never stop halfway up a single step.
analogies.mapsTo: A discrete domain: specific, separate values you can list.
analogies.because: Each step is a whole landing spot with a gap to the next, just like whole counts of tickets or people.

analogies.everydayScene: You roll up the ramp and pass through every single height between the bottom and the top, including 2.37 feet up.
analogies.mapsTo: A continuous domain: every value in an interval, written as an inequality.
analogies.because: There is no gap on the ramp, just like there is no gap between 2.37 and 2.38 gallons of water.

analogies.everydayScene: The cup is marked at 1 cup and 2 cups, but the water can sit anywhere between the marks.
analogies.mapsTo: A range with real-world limits: the amount can be anything from 0 up to the cup's capacity.
analogies.because: The cup's size caps the values, so the range stops at the top mark even though the water is continuous.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the procedure for writing domain and range: identify discrete or continuous, list or bound the values, then apply real-world limits like no negatives or a maximum capacity.

data.title: How to Write Domain and Range for a Situation
data.subtitle: Four steps, in order, every time.

steps.label: Step 1: Count or measure?
steps.text: Decide whether the situation is discrete or continuous.
steps.detail: Counting whole items (people, tickets, pages) is discrete. Measuring amounts (time, height, water, temperature) is continuous.

steps.label: Step 2: Pick the notation.
steps.text: Discrete uses a set of specific values. Continuous uses inequalities.
steps.detail: Discrete: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. Continuous: 0 <= x <= 12.

steps.label: Step 3: Apply real-world limits.
steps.text: Cross out values the situation cannot allow.
steps.detail: Time and length cannot be negative, so start at 0. A tank that holds at most 50 gallons stops at 50.

steps.label: Step 4: Write domain and range.
steps.text: Domain describes the input values; range describes the output values.
steps.detail: For a tank filling for 12 minutes at 4 gallons per minute: domain 0 <= x <= 12, range 0 <= y <= 48.

blocks.purpose: Confront the top errors: connecting dots for countable data, forgetting that time and length can't be negative, and ignoring a context cap on the domain.

data.flagIntro: These are common mistakes when graphing real situations.

cautions.title: Do not connect dots for countable data
cautions.detail: If the input only makes sense in whole steps, the graph is separate dots. A line would claim that in-between values are real, and they are not.
cautions.wrongExample: Connecting dots for number of tickets sold
cautions.exampleNote: You cannot sell 1.5 tickets, so there is no point between the dots.

cautions.title: Do not allow negative time or length
cautions.detail: Time and length cannot be negative, so check whether the domain and range should start at 0 or at a starting value.
cautions.exampleNote: The lower limit comes from the real world, not from the equation.

cautions.title: Do not ignore a context cap
cautions.detail: A tank that holds at most 50 gallons cannot have a range above 50, even if the formula keeps growing. The context sets the ceiling.
cautions.wrongExample: Range y >= 0 with no upper limit
cautions.exampleNote: The formula may keep going, but the tank does not.

blocks.purpose: Make the learner sort mixed situations (number of students, temperature, pages read, rainfall) into discrete or continuous buckets to apply the distinction.

data.title: Sort the situations
data.instruction: Drag each card into the bucket that fits: discrete for countable items, continuous for measurable amounts.

items.text: Number of students in class
Temperature outside right now
Pages read in a book
Rainfall in one hour

blocks.purpose: Have the learner type domain and range for one discrete and one continuous situation, practising set notation and inequality notation with real-world limits.

data.prompt: A school bus holds at most 45 students. Let x equal the number of students on the bus. Write the domain of x using set notation for this discrete situation.
acceptedAnswers: {x | x is a whole number, 0 <= x <= 45}
data.errorMessage: Check the set notation and limits.
data.explanation: The domain is the set of whole numbers from 0 to 45 because you cannot have a fraction of a student on the bus.

data.title: Quick Reference: Discrete vs Continuous

rows.value: Countable whole items (students, pages, cars)
Measurable amounts (time, height, temperature)
Use set braces: {0, 1, 2, ...}
Use inequalities: 0 ≤ x ≤ 12

checks.prompt: A parking lot attendant records data each hour. Which quantity should be modeled with a discrete domain?
checks.answer: The number of cars in the lot
checks.rationale: Counting cars gives separate whole-number values, so the number of cars is discrete; temperature, time, and height can take any value in an interval.
checks.hint: Ask yourself whether you count it in whole pieces or measure it with a tool.
choices: The number of cars in the lot
The total time the lot has been open
The height of the lot's sign
checks.focus: Decide whether a real situation (e.g., number of cars in a lot vs. temperature over a day) is discrete or continuous

checks.prompt: A shelf holds at most 6 books, and each book takes one spot. The number of books on the shelf is x. Write the domain as a set of values.
checks.rationale: Books are counted in whole numbers, and the shelf holds at most 6, so the possible counts are the whole numbers from 0 through 6.
checks.hint: Start at 0, since an empty shelf is possible, and stop at the most the shelf can hold.
checks.focus: Write the domain of a discrete situation as a set of whole-number values

checks.prompt: A small pool is being filled. It holds at most 50 gallons, and the number of gallons in it is g. Which inequality gives the domain for g?
checks.rationale: Gallons can be any amount from empty (0) up to the cap of 50, and both endpoints are possible, so the domain is 0 <= g <= 50.
checks.hint: The pool can be empty or full, so both ends of the range are allowed.
checks.focus: Choose the correct inequality domain for a continuous situation with a real-world cap (e.g., 0 ≤ x ≤ 50)

checks.prompt: A graph shows the number of tickets sold each day as separate points. Why is it wrong to connect the points with a line?
checks.answer: The line would show fractional ticket counts between days, which cannot happen
checks.rationale: A connected line includes every value between the points, but ticket counts are whole numbers, so the in-between values are meaningless.
checks.hint: Think about what a point halfway between two dots would represent.
choices: The line would show fractional ticket counts between days, which cannot happen
The line would make the graph too steep to read
Connecting points always changes the y-values
The points are not allowed to be graphed at all
checks.focus: Identify why connecting the dots on a discrete graph is incorrect

claims.claim: Domain and range are the same set of whole numbers from 0 to 45 because you cannot have a fraction of a student on the bus.

claims.claim: The line would show students present at times when no one was counted. (correct answer)
claims.truth: Acceptable as the best answer. A line implies in-between values that were never counted, which would be fractions of students. Check 3 gives the clearer reason, fractional counts.

claims.truth: This option is rightly wrong, because 'always' is false.

claims.claim: You must connect points to find the slope.
claims.truth: This option is rightly wrong. You can find slope (rate of change) from two points without drawing a line.

claims.claim: Slope needs a line only for continuous data
claims.truth: Slope can be computed between any two points, and discrete linear patterns have a constant slope. Arithmetic sequences, from the previous lesson, are discrete and their common difference is the slope. Replace with something like 'Slope does not require connecting the points'.

The points stand for whole numbers of students on specific days only. A line would pretend students exist at every time between days.

claims.claim: Choice 0 (marked correct): The line would show students present at times when no one was counted.

claims.claim: The count of tickets sold so far: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. There is no such thing as 2.5 tickets sold.
The amount of water in the tank: it could be 12 gallons, or 12.3 gallons, or 12.37 gallons, depending on when you look.
Both are real. The difference is whether the values come in separate steps or flow smoothly.
Discrete data: You get the values by counting whole items. There are gaps between one value and the next. Example: Number of students in a class: 24 or 25, never 24.6
Separate values: Only specific numbers make sense. Example: Pages read: 7 pages or 8 pages, not 7.5 pages
claims.truth: Acceptable as a modeling convention; a reader could technically read half a page, but for whole-item counting the model treats pages read as discrete.

claims.claim: Discrete graph look: Plot separate dots. Do not connect them, because nothing happens between the dots.
Continuous data: You get the values by measuring. Between any two values there is always another value. Example: Temperature: 71 degrees, 71.4 degrees, 71.42 degrees
Any value in an interval: Every number in the range is possible, including decimals and fractions. Example: Height of a plant: 12.5 cm is a real possible height
Continuous graph look: Plot a connected line or curve, because the in-between values are real too.
Ask yourself: do I count it or do I measure it? Counting gives separate values; measuring gives a smooth interval.
A discrete domain is a set of separate values. A continuous domain is an interval of values, written with inequalities.
The situation decides which one you use, not the numbers themselves.
A staircase maps to a discrete domain: specific, separate values you can list.
A wheelchair ramp: You roll up the ramp and pass through every single height between the bottom and the top, including 2.37 feet up.
A measuring cup: the water can sit anywhere between the marks; the cup's size caps the values, so the range stops at the top mark even though the water is continuous.
Step 1: Counting whole items (people, tickets, pages) is discrete. Measuring amounts (time, height, water, temperature) is continuous.
Step 2: Discrete uses a set of specific values. Continuous uses inequalities. Discrete: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. Continuous: 0 <= x <= 12.
Step 3: Time and length cannot be negative, so start at 0. A tank that holds at most 50 gallons stops at 50.
For a tank filling for 12 minutes at 4 gallons per minute: domain 0 <= x <= 12, range 0 <= y <= 48.
claims.truth: 4 gal/min × 12 min = 48 gallons, so the range 0 ≤ y ≤ 48 is correct.

claims.claim: Do not connect dots for countable data: If the input only makes sense in whole steps, the graph is separate dots. You cannot sell 1.5 tickets, so there is no point between the dots.
Do not allow negative time or length: A stopwatch does not run backward and a plant is not -3 cm tall. Unless the context says otherwise, start the domain and range at 0.
Do not ignore a context cap: A tank that holds at most 50 gallons cannot have a range above 50, even if the formula keeps growing.
Number of students in class is discrete.
Temperature outside right now is continuous.
Pages read in a book is discrete.
claims.truth: Consistent with the lesson's whole-item counting model; acceptable at this level.

claims.claim: Rainfall in one hour is continuous.
A school bus holds at most 45 students. Domain: {0,1,2,...,45}; Range: {0,1,2,...,45}.
Explanation: Domain and range are the same set of whole numbers from 0 to 45 because you cannot have a fraction of a student on the bus.
Correct answer: The line would show students present at times when no one was counted.
Wrong option: Connecting points always makes the graph easier to read.
claims.truth: Correctly marked wrong: connecting discrete points misrepresents the data regardless of readability.

claims.claim: Wrong option: The line would only work if the data were temperatures instead.
claims.truth: Correctly marked wrong: the reason connecting is wrong here is the discrete counts, not a general rule about temperature graphs.

claims.claim: Wrong option: You must connect points to find the slope.
claims.truth: Correctly marked wrong: slope is not a reason to connect discrete data points.

claims.claim: The points stand for whole numbers of students on specific days only. A line would pretend students exist at every time between days.
Discrete data: Countable whole items (students, pages, cars).
Continuous data: Measurable amounts (time, height, temperature).
Discrete notation: Use set braces: {0, 1, 2, ...}.
Continuous notation: Use inequalities: 0 ≤ x ≤ 12.
Real limits check: No negatives for people, time, length; cap at max capacity.
Answer: The number of cars in the lot is the discrete quantity; temperature, time, and height are continuous.
Answer: {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} for the number of books on a shelf holding at most 6 books.
Answer: 0 <= g <= 50 for gallons in a pool holding at most 50 gallons; both endpoints are possible.
Wrong options: 0 < g < 50, g >= 50, g <= 0 are all incorrect for this situation.

claims.claim: Answer: The line would show fractional ticket counts between days, which cannot happen.
Wrong options: 'The line would make the graph too steep to read', 'Connecting points always changes the y-values', 'The points are not allowed to be graphed at all'.
claims.truth: All three are correctly marked wrong; the real reason is that in-between values are meaningless for whole ticket counts.

plans.approach: A typical 14-year-old learns this best by seeing absolute value as distance, then splitting into AND vs OR with a clear contrast and worked steps before practicing. The lesson confronts the classic split/negation error directly and ends with a memory anchor plus a real tolerance context.
coverage: Absolute value as distance from zero; |x| = a splits into x = a or x = -a
|x| < a and |x| ≤ a become AND compound inequalities: -a < x < a (a bounded interval)
|x| > a and |x| ≥ a become OR compound inequalities: x < -a or x > a (two rays)
Solve multi-step absolute value inequalities by isolating the absolute value first, then splitting
Graph solutions on a number line: open vs closed endpoints, shading between vs shading outward
Flip the inequality direction when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Recognize no-solution cases like |x| < -3 and all-real cases like |x| > -3
Translate tolerance/error contexts (|x - c| ≤ t) into an interval and interpret its meaning
Common error: forgetting to negate and flip when splitting, or writing a single inequality instead of a compound one

blocks.purpose: Pose a real manufacturing tolerance choice (a part within 0.5 mm of spec) so the learner feels why 'distance from a target' needs its own inequality form.

data.prompt: A machinist must make a bolt 40 mm long. The customer will accept any bolt whose length is within 0.5 mm of 40 mm. Which rule should the inspector use to decide if a bolt passes?
data.context: The inspector measures one bolt at 39.4 mm and another at 40.6 mm. Both are 0.6 mm away from the target of 40 mm. The shop needs one inequality that captures 'close enough to 40' in a single statement.

leftChoice.label: OPTION A
leftChoice.title: Two separate checks
leftChoice.body: Pass the bolt if length ≥ 39.5 and length ≤ 40.5. Two conditions, both must hold.

rightChoice.label: OPTION B
rightChoice.title: One distance check
rightChoice.body: Pass the bolt if |length - 40| ≤ 0.5. One statement about distance from the target.

data.footerNote: Both rules describe the same set of acceptable bolts. The distance form is shorter, and it is exactly what absolute value inequalities are built to express.

blocks.purpose: Anchor the core rule: |x| < a means distance less than a, giving the AND interval -a < x < a, with the three prerequisite facts (absolute value = distance, splitting, endpoint inclusion).

data.anchor: |x| < a means the distance from x to 0 is less than a, so x sits between -a and a: -a < x < a.
prerequisites: Absolute value measures distance from zero, so |x| is never negative. For example, |-7| = 7 and |7| = 7.
An equation like |x| = 5 splits into two cases: x = 5 or x = -5, because both 5 and -5 are 5 units from zero.
A strict inequality (< or >) uses an open endpoint, and a non-strict inequality (≤ or ≥) uses a closed endpoint.
The symbol a stands for a positive number here. If a is negative, the rule needs a separate look, which comes later in this lesson.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side contrast of |x| < a (AND, between) versus |x| > a (OR, outside) so the learner sees the two solution shapes and why they differ.

data.title: Less Than vs Greater Than: Two Different Shapes
data.subtitle: Same absolute value, opposite inequality symbol, completely different solution set.

items.label: Shape
items.text: The solutions are trapped between two numbers, so you write one compound inequality joined by AND.
items.example: |x| < 4 gives -4 < x < 4

items.label: Why AND
items.text: A number must be close to zero on both sides at once. It has to satisfy both pieces simultaneously.
items.example: x = 1 works because 1 > -4 AND 1 < 4

items.label: Graph
items.text: Shade the segment between the endpoints. Open circles for < and >, filled circles for ≤ and ≥.
items.example: |x| ≤ 4 shades from -4 to 4 with filled endpoints

items.label: Endpoints
items.text: The endpoints themselves are not solutions for a strict inequality, because their distance equals a, not less than a.
items.example: |4| < 4 is false, since 4 is not less than 4

items.label: Shape
items.text: The solutions run off in two directions, so you write two separate inequalities joined by OR.
items.example: |x| > 4 gives x < -4 or x > 4

items.label: Why OR
items.text: A number only needs to be far from zero on one side. Satisfying either piece is enough.
items.example: x = 9 works because 9 > 4, even though 9 is not less than -4

items.label: Graph
items.text: Shade two rays pointing outward from the endpoints, with a gap in the middle.
items.example: |x| ≥ 4 shades left of -4 and right of 4, filled endpoints

items.label: The gap
items.text: Numbers between -4 and 4 fail, because their distance from zero is less than 4.
items.example: x = 0 fails |x| > 4

data.footnote: Less than: shade between the endpoints. Greater than: shade outward, away from zero.

blocks.purpose: Lay out the solve procedure in order: isolate the absolute value, split into the two cases, flip direction when dividing by a negative, then graph.

data.title: Solving an Absolute Value Inequality in Five Steps
data.subtitle: Worked on 3|x - 2| + 1 ≤ 13.

steps.label: Step 1: Isolate the absolute value
steps.text: Undo everything outside the bars using inverse operations, exactly as you would for an equation.

steps.label: Step 2: Read the symbol to pick the shape
steps.text: A less-than symbol (or less-than-or-equal) means BETWEEN, so you build an AND chain. A greater-than symbol means OUTSIDE, so you build two rays joined by OR.
steps.detail: Here the symbol is ≤, so the answer is a single interval between two numbers.

steps.label: Step 3: Split, negating the right side
steps.text: Drop the bars and write the inside between -4 and 4. The negative case always uses the opposite of the number on the right.

steps.label: Step 4: Solve the compound and flip if needed
steps.text: Add, subtract, multiply, or divide every part of the chain. If you multiply or divide by a negative, flip both inequality symbols.
steps.detail: Add 2 to all three parts: -2 ≤ x ≤ 6. No division by a negative, so no flip.

steps.label: Step 5: Graph and check
steps.text: Shade between the endpoints with filled circles for ≤. Test one value inside and one outside to confirm.

blocks.purpose: Map the decision path from an absolute value inequality to its compound form, including the no-solution (|x| < negative) and all-real (|x| > negative) branches.

data.title: Which Compound Form Does It Take?
data.subtitle: Follow the decision path from an isolated absolute value inequality to its solution shape.

nodes.label: Isolated: |inside| (symbol) a
nodes.detail: Bars alone on one side, a number a on the other

nodes.label: Is a negative?
nodes.detail: Look at the number on the right of the symbol

nodes.label: |x| < negative
nodes.detail: Distance can never be less than a negative number

nodes.label: |x| > negative
nodes.detail: Every distance is greater than a negative number

nodes.label: Which symbol?
nodes.detail: Less-than or greater-than

nodes.label: AND: -a < inside < a
nodes.detail: Between the endpoints, one shaded segment

nodes.label: OR: inside < -a or inside > a
nodes.detail: Outside the endpoints, two shaded rays

nodes.label: Solve each part, flip on negative division
nodes.detail: Then graph with open or closed endpoints

data.footer: The two negative branches are the special cases. A distance is never negative, so |x| < -3 has no solution, while |x| > -3 is true for every real number.

blocks.purpose: Target the #1 mistake: forgetting to negate and flip when splitting, or collapsing an OR into a single inequality, with feedback on why intuition fails.

data.question: Which compound inequality is the correct solution to |x - 5| > 3?
data.context: A classmate writes -3 < x - 5 < 3 and calls it done.
data.commonErrorLabel: Collapsing an OR into a single chain

trapReasons.1: This is the AND shape. It comes from a less-than symbol, but the problem has a greater-than symbol.
trapReasons.2: The endpoints are right, but the directions are reversed. The outside pieces are x < 2 and x > 8, not x < 8 and x > 2.
trapReasons.3: This is the split for |x - 5| < 3. The greater-than symbol needs the outside form, not the between form.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: Some students write one chain, like the between form they just practised. But 'distance greater than 3' means far from 5 in either direction, so the answer has to be two separate rays. Writing a chain forces the answer to be between the numbers, which is the opposite of what the symbol asks.
data.correctReasoning: |x - 5| > 3 means the distance from x to 5 is more than 3. So x is more than 3 units to the right of 5, or more than 3 units to the left. That gives x - 5 > 3 or x - 5 < -3. Solving each: x > 8 or x < 2. Check x = 0: |0 - 5| = 5 > 3, true. Check x = 5: |5 - 5| = 0 > 3, false, and 5 is indeed not in the solution.
data.recoveryTip: Before splitting, say the symbol out loud. 'Greater than' means outside, so write OR and two rays. 'Less than' means between, so write AND and one chain. Then always negate the right side in the second case.

blocks.purpose: Have the learner type the compound inequality and interval for several absolute value inequalities, applying the split rule themselves.

data.prompt: Solve |x + 1| < 6 and write the solution as a compound inequality in the form a < x < b.
data.context: Split the absolute value into an AND chain first, then subtract 1 from all three parts.
data.successMessage: Correct. |x + 1| < 6 becomes -6 < x + 1 < 6, and subtracting 1 from every part gives -7 < x < 5.
data.errorMessage: Not quite. Split into -6 < x + 1 < 6, then subtract 1 from all three parts.
data.explanation: The less-than symbol means between, so the answer is one AND chain. Subtracting 1 from -6, x + 1, and 6 gives -7 < x < 5. Test x = 0: |0 + 1| = 1 < 6, true. Test x = 6: |6 + 1| = 7 < 6, false.

blocks.purpose: Show a tolerance/error case (|x - c| ≤ t) and interpret the solution as an acceptable range, connecting the algebra to a real measurement.

data.ruleName: Tolerance as an Absolute Value Inequality
data.headline: Under this example's rule, a tablet 8 mg off is rejected
data.caseText:
Suppose a quality standard allows the actual amount x in a 500 mg tablet to differ from 500 mg by at most 5 mg, or the tablet is rejected.
Written as an inequality, the acceptable amount x satisfies |x - 500| ≤ 5. That means the distance from x to 500 is at most 5.
Splitting gives -5 ≤ x - 500 ≤ 5, and adding 500 to all three parts gives 495 ≤ x ≤ 505. Any tablet between 495 mg and 505 mg passes; anything outside that window is pulled from the batch.

metric.label: width of the acceptable window, from 495 mg to 505 mg

data.consequenceMissed: Without the interval, a tablet at 508 mg looks 'close to 500' and ships, even though it is 8 mg off and outside the allowed range in this example.
data.consequenceApplied: The interval turns a vague 'close enough' into a hard cutoff, so every tablet is either inside 495 to 505 mg or rejected.
data.sourceNote: Pharmacies and manufacturers use percentage tolerance limits on tablet content, and this example is simplified.

blocks.purpose: Give a compact memory anchor: 'less than is between (AND), greater than is outside (OR), and always negate-and-flip the second case.'

data.title: The Split Rule in One Line
data.anchor: Less than between, greater outside; negate and flip the second side.
data.subtitle: Two ideas: which shape to draw, and how to handle the negative side.

expansions.phrase: |x| < a gives -a < x < a, one shaded segment joined by AND
|x| > a gives x < -a or x > a, two shaded rays joined by OR
The second case always uses the opposite of the number on the right
In the second case, negate the number and reverse the symbol. Also reverse the symbols when you multiply or divide by a negative.

data.rationale: The first half of the rhyme picks the shape from the symbol, and the second half protects you from two common errors: dropping the negative and forgetting to reverse the symbol.

blocks.purpose: Summarize all rules in one matrix: the four inequality forms, their compound equivalents, graph shape, and the two special cases.
